Our Royal Family is not only the cheapest the country has ever had, brit it is also the most inexpensive in the world. The entire expense of the whole British Royal Family amounts to only £165,000 a I ear, for against the total espenditute of £530,000 must be set the rec(ipt of £415,000 from Crown lands, leaving the above net cost. On the Queen's accession, the nation took ever the Crown !arias paying instead a fixed annual sum to Her Majesty. The value of these lands has increased so much during her reign that bad thy retnained in her possession,the Sovereign would be the wealthiest person in the country. All the most valuable Ltnd ia London, worth £3000,000 an acre, is Crown land. Out of the chaos which descend' d from the days of George IV., a method was evolved by Her Majesty and the late Prince Consort, which entirely and absolutely does away with waste and extravagance in housekeep- ing, and in this, as in so many other directions, the Queen has set an example, all women in their different stations would do well to follow. The books are most methodically and minutely kept, the whole vast estab- lishment as methodically conducted as any great business.

Lady Salisbury continues to improve, to the great re- lief of her family, and the delight of her many friends. With the romance connected with her marriage, most of us are familiar. The late Lord Salisbuey put many obstacles in the way of the match which he considered unsuitable, but the lovers stood all tests, and Lord Robert Cecil, as he was then, obtained a wife whose compatibility of disposilon has made his domestic life as pure and peaceful as that of any public man of our time. Lady Salisbury is a strong minded practical woman, and a repartee which survives in some me- moirs will show how sharp is her intellect. After Lord Cranborne—as her husband had then become—had re- signed office, along with Lord Carnarvon. and General Peel, OR account of the Reform Bill of 1867, Lord Derby asked her if she remained awake all night, like Cran- borne, calculating the effects' of the Bill. "Yes" she said, "I was engaged in a sum uf subtraction, and I found that if you took three from twelve (the number of the Cabinet) nothing remained." The London season of 1899 must now be numbered among those past and gone. . The last night was taken by Lady Ilchester, whose ball at Holland House was a most brilliant function. Holland House is one of the most interesting mansions in London. When one enters its gilded gates and sees the statue of the famous Henry Fox, a memory of past diplomatic and literary grandeur seems to fill the air, and it has had more than one not- able owner. The library is where Addison (who married the widowed Lady Holland, and who died here) uoed to pace up slid down and take a glass of port from a bottle placed by a footman at either end,and it was here the late Lady Holland gave her political, literary, and artistic garden parties, which have never,in peint of in- terest, been equalled in the present generation. The polished floors, tbe beautiful pictures and china ,and the lovely gardens make it quite a paradise even among the smuts and dirt, of London. Before the death of the Duke of Clarence, the last night of the London Season was held sacred to the Prince and Princess of Wales, who invariably gave a grand ball on this particular occasion, at Marltorough House. On March 10th their Royal Highnesses were wont too.to celebrate the anniversary of their wedding in a similar manner, and at Sandringham, the magnificent ballroom built by the Prince of Wales was the scene each winter of three principal balls—the County, the Tenants, and the Servants. To the County came all the elite of the district, and the market town of Lynn could not find accommodation for the guests. Every available bed in the villages adjacent to Sandringham had to be called into requisition. But all these festivkties, have long since ceased, a state of affairs deplored by not a few. Happy indeed are those who do not give evidence of their high temperature. Given a tremendous heat to start with, it makes one hotter still to meet folks with damp, claret-coloured faces, and uncurled hair. The coolest looking individual I have met during the past week or so, was a girl dressed in pa'e blue cotton, quite simply and loosely made. She carried a dark blue sun- shade, which looked delightful. Per hot weather, red, bright blue, and all vivid colours, are very effective for sunshades, but for almost tropical da3s, a dark blue specimen is far better. The very coolest sunshades are those of some dark colour, blue, brown, or green, lined with very pale green chiffon, which is notoriously cool looking, and which with the darker naaterial,forms a mat effectual and effective shield from the sun. The pal, r shades do not caq that ghastly tint on the face which green im- parts, while they certainly do not increase the colour. Once again comes the repeated rumor that white stockings will be worn by the best dressed women, with toilettes of every description. What a strange resolution it would be, if, in conjunction with wtete stockings, we were also to a& pt the square-teed, flat-soled sandals, likewise beloved of our grandmothers. It would be necessary to abandon the fiction which we all now do our utmost to maintain, that our feet end in a single central, and sharply-pointed toe, but once having admit- ted that the true shape of our feet demands a shoe end- ing with a width of at least an inch and a half, for the accommodetion of two toes of nearly equal length, a much more graceful gait and carriage than most of us can now command, would tea result. In such a shoe, the foot could be firmly put to the ground, and we should not need to use it in .a gingerly manrer, mindful to tread only on the less resentful part of it. If we would'keep our footgear in good condition, we must first and foremost provide curselves with as many trees as boots and shoes. This sounds extravagant, but in the long run the plan will be found to be an economi- cal one. The trees which can now be obtained at a very low figure, indeed, should be placed in the boots, or shoes, so anon as they are taken off, and the footgear laced or buttoned over them. If wet, boots and shoes should not be dried by artificel heat, and not cleaned until quite dry. If they have become very wet, and are hard when dry, a little sweet oil or vaseline rubbed well in will soften ~the leather and prevent it cracking. Kid, or patent leather should never to used in hot weather. If once they get thoroughly wet they never recover,however carefully treated. Spanish women bear the palm in having the smallest feet in the world. Those of the Peruvian and Chilian women make a good second and third. The feet of American women are not particularly small,hut are well shaped, and always perfectly shod. The Russians on the contrary, have heavy clumsy feet. The best shaped feet are always to be found in Southern Europe, and of those in the North, the Swedish and German hold the first position. In this country it is more the fault of our shoemakere that our feet are not fascinating in appear- ance.
" MADGE."

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MT DRAB NELLIE,

A hat a frieud was wearing recently was admired very much by me. It was composed of a delicious shade of grey straw turned up slightly at the lefb side. The ornament for the most part consisted of white marguerites, chiffon and roses. The great charm of the sailor hat is heightened a thousand- fold by the presence of a scarf of lace in corn-fiower blue colouring, draped round the low crown and tied in a loose bow at the left side. Here its fringed ends overhang the brim, which should be tip-tilted in jaunty fashion by means of a bow of black velvet underneath. A long quill caught through the scarf in front may also be worn.

I notice there are still some of those charm- ing sailor blouses made in silk about. The collar is edged with a kilted frill of white and fastened with a loosely knotted scarf and the vest and collar are in white silk all tucked. I have seen a good many blouses, notably one in white silk with an insertion and applique of yellowish lace, and clever touches of black velvet baby•ribbon on shirred chiffon. The same design can be carried out in pale blue. But one of the most attractive of all is the blouse of white silk finely tucked both at the back and in front, and provided with a yoke, collar and cuffs of transparent lace. As this is perhaps the garment of all others which is in demand this season you can appreciate the attractiveness of its appearance.

The other day I saw a lovely costume of grey cloth. The double breasted coat was provided With a big collar of white silk embroidered with a scroll and floral design in black ribbon and yellows ,lab lace. It had groups of steel buttons at either side. Recently I saw a costume which was a veritable triumph of satorial art. It had an elaborate arrangement of stitching and its pipings of white satin added a nice finish to the flounces of the beautifully hanging skirt. It practically covered the coat which boasted of collar ; revers of white satin' embroidered with an appliqué of grey-green cloth and chenille, glittering here and there with decorative little buttons. The cloth, grass-green in colour, was of a soft texture, and the lining throughout was of silk.

A lady I met the other day was wearing a white straw hat, with a true lovere knot bow of black velvet to hold in bondage. Pink roses trailed round the crown, and a smaller bow assisted some half-blown roses to tilt the brim up at the left side. For a background I suggest that sunshade of black and white silk, whose checked pattern is visible through the lining of chiffon. This is only one of many other pretty things of the same kind to be seen.

If you would only brush your clothes when you take them off, instead of waiting until the next day, they would last twice as long again. Failing this, it is best to shake them well before putting them away. I make it a rule to take off my dress the moment I come in, and step into an indoor frock. Ido not say a tea-gown, because I consider they are lazy garments and are ill-suited to an ener- getic nature,. My shoes are changed, not for slippers, which I consider perdition to a woman's feet, but for some older house shoes. When you are making a dross at home, please remember that it is al-ways best to allow for turn- ings. Have a good cut-to-measure bodice pattern in lining or brown holland to start on. When the bodice lining is fitted, care must be taken to get the waist line in its proper place so pin a tape round the 'waist to mark the place of the belt webbing. A bodice, if properly cut for a normal figure, will only require altering on the shoulder and under arm seams. Tile fronts must never be brought forward towards the neck, but rather be smoothed away towards the shoulder, else the chest will have a contracted appearance. For this reason I find it an excellent plan to pad the bust when having a dress fitted at a dressmaker's. The neck can be measured in the same way as the waist- band. I shall be pleased to give you other hints another week.
Your loving JENICIIL
'OLYPITON.

div.head: INNER MAN.
div.p: THE INNER MAN.

The men whe do our thinking for us have dis- covered in many out-of-the-way places the sources of great political, social, and industrial movements, but it does not appear that any of them ever thought of looking into the kitchen for the genesis of revelutiou. We have become so accustomed to the intellectual bide of man, that we often forget his materiality. That the change in the public policy of a nation should follow a banquet seems to be a result enor- mously disproportionate to the cause, yet nothing is more certain than the fact that the banquet and the dinner are prime factors in the business and political, as well as social circles of the day. To appeal to the digestive rather than to the in tellectual apparatus of a lord of creation seems to place humanity on the level of the brute, but how- ever high the grade of civilisation to which man may attain, the animal nature is the foundation on which the intellectual is reared.

Never was there a man so gifted of mind,so spiri- tual of soul, as not to feel the pangs of hunger. The philosopher must leave his speculations and eat ; the statesman must drop the consideration of public policies when lunch time comes around ; and the preacher, however devoted he may be to the care of souls, gives his anxious heart temporary re- spite at meal times. Men who have objects to attain find their wits sharpened by their anxiety, and thus it is that the dinner has from time immemorial been employee as a means of persuasion. An end in itself, it has been diverted from its original intent to a purpose quite legitimate, and yet, not recog- nised by the unknown founder of the custom. With him who is hungry, " the time is out of joint," he quarrels with his partner, scolds his wife, slaps the childten, he feels that his new coat does not fit, that the old pain in his back is certain to develop into incurable disease, that his shoes pinch, that his collar rubs his neck, that, in short, human existence is a hollow mockery, and if it were not for his family he would cheerfully get out of it. A halt hour spent in communion with his dinner works a miracle. With the first spoonful of soup a change colues o'er him. ills cellar is perfectly com- fortable, and his shoes ore as easy as ten-year-old slippers. With the roast beef and potatoes, he lis- teus with dignified satisfaction to his wife's account of the people who have just moved in next door, and is gratified that her mentally taken inventory of their furniture, itemised as it was carried from the wagon, showed its inferiority, both in quantity and quality, to his own.

As he ii;iits his after-dinner cigar, he panses a moment and half turns round before the mirror to notice with complacent self-gratulation how well his coat sets in the back then sits down in an easy chair contented and happy. He who decries eating speaks az one without understanding. Eating is one of the greatest busi- nesses in the world. He who said "'tie love that makes the world go round" was mistaken. It is not love, but a desire to eat that causes our planet to revolve. In comparison as incentives with the desire to eat, ambition, the craving for power, the longing for place and preferment, are but minor and subsidiary considerations.

"La granola"- passion" must itself yield to hunger for although modern novelists, no more than the writers of old-time romances, make mention of their heroes eating, the omission is merely in defer- ence to public opinion, which is universally agreed that the lover ought to be above eating. There is nothing aesthetic about the dinner table; it can- not be utilised, save incidentally, in the develop- ment of a plct. Three-fourths of the world's effort is devoted, not to heaping up weal•h, but to getting something to eat. If men could live without eating, life would have no problems. for the human race could easily keep out of the ftigid zones, and, under temperate or equatorial skies, the raiment invented ty Mrs. Eve would be adequate, and the primitive abode quite sufficient. But men wanted to eat,and what is more, they wanted to eat good things, so they worked.

It is plain, therefore, that the principal agent in the promotion of the world's civilisation is not poetry, nor art, not philosophy nor science, but hunger. The men who have money are courted by those who want money; not fcr itself, but that they may use it to buy something to eat. seeing then the potency of the stomach in society and state, in businei,s and politics, even in " affairs du coeur," it is not without reason that men who have objects to gain, undertake to achieve them by working first upon the appetite,: then upon the in- tellect.

The present popularity of the dinner is a revival, for in ages prior to our own the value of the banquet as a factor in politics was as well known as it is among us. The school books and histories inspire the mistaken belief that the costly dinners and suppers given by mediaeval kings at their coronations, by Roman emperors at the festivals of the gods, were merely for the purpose of enabling the guests to exercise their love of gluttony and gratify the vaingloriousness of the giver. But this was fur from the true state of affairs. As a matter of fact, they were given for exactly the same purpose that the wife has in view when pre- paring an extra pie or pudding to wheedle money from her not-overgenerous spouse. Human nature does not change Kr much from age to age as might be supposed. There is no reason to doubt that the motives which actuate men now, the love of place, the desire for power, are the same that they were in the earliest stages of society, and no one need be surprised if, when the Babylonish discoveries are completed, record will be found of a political dinner given in the Temple of Belus 7,000 years before Christ.—Science Siftings.

div.head: REVENGE OF VALERIE:
div.p: REVENGE OF VALERIE:
A ROMANCE OF BRITISH COLUMBIA.
BY HUME NISBET,
Author of "A Sweet Sinner," "Bail Up," "The Rebel Chief," "Kings of the Sea," "Hunting for Gold, "The Swampers," &c.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Sir Lewis Eastlake, twenty-four years of age, is introduced to the reader, as he is "going the pace," at a London gambling club. There, in company with a friend, Captain Eric St. Arnoul, he gets ir to an altercation,which results in a duel, at Cherbourg. His opponent is killed in this. He has a strong sentimental friendship with the Duchess of Valerie, at Genoa, a widow lady, in the prime of her beauty, who, in affection for him, backs the financier, who lends him money. Captain St. Arnoul, his com- panion, who is a cousin of the Duchess, informs her that Sir Lewis had been injured in the duel, and, in view of the other_man's death, it is thought prudent he should be removed from Cherbourg. The Duchess hears that he is in charge of a Cherbourg doctor, who is an old friend, and his sister,who is a nurse. She fears that he may be arrested, and arranges with the Captain for him to be taken by the nurse to her seat at Falaise, and she follows on afterwards.

div.head: CHAPTER V. IN TIIE GLOAMING.
div.p: CHAPTER V. IN TIIE GLOAMING.

There was nothing particularly striking in the lady who faced the Duchess, beyond the fact that she was a lady, and young, instead of being, as her grace had supposed, elderly. She was young, fair-haired, unmistakably grace- ful in her figure and movements, but rather pale- faced and wearied-looking with her late vigils. The Duchess looked at the other with frozen astonishment for a moment, then she resumed her presence of mind and advanced smilingly towards the invalid. "I did not expect to fini you up yet, Lewis."

Sir Lewis Eastlake reclined against some soft cushions, and looked wan and troubled. He could not yet move without assistance, but be smiled faintly as he raised his left hand slowly. He had been hit in the right shoulder, therefore could not raise that side.

"Thanks to your goodness, Valerie, and the care my friend here has taken of me, I was able to sit up, and welcome you home." 'How do you do, Miss Waldred ? Do you know, you have surprised me greatly? " "Why, your grace ? " asked the young lady quietly, in a sweet, soft voice. The Duchess laughed a little foolishly as she answered: "Well, I expected to find a lady of more mature age, or I should hardly have trusted you with such a charge." "I am twenty-three, and have had a good deal of experience in nursing, madam." "Forgive me my first surprise, my dear Miss Waldred. I can see from your tired expression that you have devoted yourself to your duty. Now that I have come, however, I shall be able to help you." With a few more of the words which social politeness dictated, the Duchess left the roQm to prepare for dinner; as she withdrew she placed her hand on the arm of Captain St. Arnoul, who waited near the door, and took him with her. She walked with him, smiling but silent, until they reached her drawing-room door. 'Then she turned suddenly and fairly hissed in his startled ears: "Fool! Why did you not tell me before I left Cherbourg tint Miss Waldred was a young woman ? " "Because I didn't know, Valerie," stammered the poor blackleg. "How could I when I had not seen her ? "

"I suppose not," she sneered viciously. "You never seem to see anything outside a pack of cards or a roulette table. I expect that you have spent -the past week mooning about my estate with a gun and a dog, while that young woman has been 'amusing your friend. That's the way to win an annuity, isn't it? " "Why, Valerie, you don't mean to say that you are going to be jealous of that doctor's colourless sister? Why, she is nothing more in his estimation than the housekeeper! She hardly speaks a word; besides, only to-day when your wire came, she announced her pleasure at your return, as she can now get back to Cherbourg." "Is this certain, Eric? " "On my honour as a gentleman," replied her cousin calmly. "Good; I will relieve her of her duty, and she may depart to-morrow. You are right; she looks a cold-blooded thing, with her sickly face and washed out eyes. I pardon you this time, Eric, only I wish she had been older. Never mind, I will trust your word that there is no damage done to—your prospects." When the door was closed behind the Duchess and Eric St. Arnoul, the lady nurse went quickly over to the couch where Sir Lewis Eastlake reclined, and bending over him she whispered: "0 Lewis! -why did you persuade me to do this thing? I have ruined you, for the Duchess loves you and would have freed you from all your troubles, but for me." "Nonsense, Hope; the Duchess may have a slight penchant toward me, but she will fly at much higher game for her next mate. You lmve made me pretty vain by giving your heart to such a ruined, dis- solute beggar as I am, but the: eis a limit to my conceit. No, dearest; her grace is good-natt red, .kind-hearted, and fond of a little harmless flirtation, but it is a prince at the least who will induce her to change her present title." He spoke reassuringly, as he fondled her hand in his left one; yet she was -not convinced. "You are wrong, Lewis; women are never deceived in those matters as men sometimes are..

• "When the Duchess entered this room, I saw the true love light in her eyes, and I also saw some- thing else when she stopped and looked at me. You have missed a great chance, you foolish, foolish boy." The invalid laughed faintly as he replied: "It has always been my fate to throw away chances, all except one, which I prize more than an El Dorado. That chance I caught in a hurry the evening before my duel. Do you regret it, Hope? —my Hope—the Hope that may yet help me to conquer the fortune I have so rashly flung away." "No, my darling. I shall never regret the step I took that night, except for your sake. But—you must tell your hostess all—without delay, and I must go home to my brother's, for I cannot stay in this house under false colours."

••-• vv.., v She stooped and kissed him lightly on the lips, then passed her fingers through his hair. She was no longer a pallid-faced woman, but a blushing girl, with lovely humid, moist blue eyes in which hung unshed tears. "Yes, perhaps you had better return to Cher- bourg, until I break the news, my dear. Mean- time, I think I shall go to,bed." •She became the careful nurse once more at this • request,' and ringing the bell, two of the male servants came in and assisted him to his feet, and up to his bedroom.

That night as the Duchess Valerie looked at her- self in the mirror, and contrasted her matchless symmetry and flashing beauty with the points of her temporary guest, she gave a sigh of supreme satisfaction. Although not too tall for grace, she was 'nearly two inches taller than Miss Waldred, which gave her a vast advantage in dress, pose, and walleing qualities. Both young ladies were slender and lithesome, but the widow was younger than the maiden, freer in 1-er actions, as well as more accomplished and wittier. Valerie had the exquisite freshness of a blush rose, while Hope looked like a faded lily beside her. In every way she surpassed the shy doctor's sister;, in features as well as in form ; in the mass and length of her tresses—she.had artfully coaxed the nurse info her chamber before retiring in ordcr to study her caref ally. She had persuaded Hope to unfast en her hair so that she might judge how long and thick it was, and felt content with the result of her investigation. Her momentary jealousy and fears were ground- less. There could be positively no danger in the presence of that insignificant stranger, while she was there, to extinguish with her overpowering lustre the other's feeble prettiness. Indeed she would have been sorry, only that she desired the field entirely to herself, that Hope was leaving so soon, she made such a capital foil. -Under the circumstances however she did not press her guest very warmly to extend her visit. !Sir Lewis was out of all danger and the fracture was almost mended. He no longer required night watching, and another week's rest would make him as strong as ever. The Duchess felt really grateful now to this girl for the care she had taken of the invalid, and was hurt that the present of jewellery which she tried to force upon her was gently but firmly refused.
"i have only done my duty to an old friend," said Hope, as she declined the proffered gift.. "Have you known Sir Lewis long ? "

*"lslnce -we were children. We were neighbours, and my brother was his first tutor in chemistry and botany., ' "Indeed!" The Duchess, in her infatuation and sense of superiority, did not feel at all uneasy to learn this. Of o irse, Lewis must havei many old friends that she knew nothing about yet. A glance at her mirror convinced her that he could have no old friends who could compete with her. What man could pass over those blue-black rippling tresses, fragrant and silky, for such light-brown stuff as that? Who could gaze into her velvety dark orbs and forget them in such colourless eyes? She was made for love, and the other, with her mild, irregular comeliness for what she said herself —passionless duty. Hope read this favoured child of Fortune and, Nature like an open book as she watched her quietly and seriously; she read her infatuation and her self-complacency with commiseration, even while she wondered that. she had been preferred toi this rich and lovely girl. So far Hope read, becatise the Duchess was revealing the childish side of her nature. But what was hidden at this time—the intensity, keenness and passionate depth of the early-developed woman—fortunately for the pen c 3 of mind of Hope, she went away withut being able to plumb. Doubtless. when all was going well with the love affairs of Lucretia Borgia in her youth, she ap- peared a very charming and innocent young lady even to her own sex.

The f hoe inc morning Hope departed to Cher- bourg, and in the afternoon Captain Eric St. Arnoul went his way to have a short but merry fling at the tables of Monte Carlo. He apologised profusely to his friend for leaving him at this time, pat on a sad air and spoke about a man he had to arrange business with in Paris—the usual business, cash raising. Sir Lewis excused him, for he also was editating very seriously about where and how he could do the same description of business. The next few days were very happy ones for the youn 1. and enamoured Duchess. Every day the baro 'et recovered strength under her generous and teneer treatment, and very soon he was able to spend the day with her, and drive about the country. He had heard of his antagonist's death, and while this filled him with deep remorse, he knew that England was no place for him. He must see fortune elsewhere.

He had written to his solicitor for a statement of his affairs, and also to Mr. Stephen Belwood to see if he could have any further advances. I is lawyer's reply settled his mind respecting En land. He was no longer a landed proprietor, nor, ine(d, was he a proprietor of anything. The mortgagee had foreclosed and seized every- thing. His name had been struck off the books of the Calydon Club, and to all intents and purposes he was an outcast.

"It's Columbia, if I can raise the necessary funds," I e muttered. "I wonder what Belwood will say." Stephen Belwood proved to be more generous than Sir Lewis expected. He offered to advance him five thousand more on condition that Sir Lewis could find a good security to back his bill. The Duchess had arranged this with her agent. Intending to get Eric to find a bogus name to Booth Ihe scruples of his trusting friend, she had meant to instruct Eric on this matter, guessing that the two friends would most likely consult together. But, having no money difficulties of her own, in her joy at having Lewis all to herself she had allowed Eric to depart without telling him any- thing about it. If she had done so affairs might have been different. As it was, however, the baronet would have considered the debt-burdened and impecunious Eric St. Arnoul's name as the very last to have on the back of a bill as security. Had the blackleg been at Falaise Sir Lewis would have shewn him the money-lender's offer and discussed the matter. But he was away, therefore the ruined young spendthrift had only his own thoughts to fall back upon. These were gloomy and perplexing thoughts which occupied his7mind, morning, noon and night. He never thought of making a confidante of his charming hostess. He could not have accepted her aid; her sex precluded any idea of that. Only one man could help him now, and it seemed too base to draw that man in, with his unlikely prospects and the 'other's circumscribed means. This was his old friend and the brother of Hope, Dr. Waldred.

How bitterly the landless baronet now regretted his former mad extravagance. We generally regret those giddy times when it is too late. He was so preoccupied and gloomy with these heavy thoughts that all the charming wiles and open hints of the Duchess were completely wasted. Chance after chance she gave him without avail. The most obtuse of intellects must have taken up the least of her obvious suggestions, but Sir Lewis still remained blind. Long drives were wasted. Walks in sheltered and lonely groves ending without avail. They had days and evenings of nztant intercourse, and still they were only friends as before, she the openly adoring, and he the gloomy indifferent. At last just when she had made up her mind to take the place of the man.and rescue him in spite of himself he resolved to tell her something of what he had been keeping back. It was that witching hour when daylight is fading and people generally feel impelled to speak their secrets—that half-hour before the lamps are lit. They had been sitting together at the window of the drawing-room, and outside the red-leaved woods were sombre and dark. They had both been silent for some time; she trying to shape plain words without quite losing her sex 'f3 privilege, he also thinking on what he had to tell her. At last he spoke in a husky voice that thrilled her through and through. It seemed to her that passion alone could make him so hoarse. "Valerie, I have a confession to wake to you. Will you listen to me ? " "Yes, Lewis," she murmured softly, getting closer to him on the couch.
At this moment the servant appeared to light the lamps. Valerie sprang up impatiently and cried: "I shall ring when we want light."
CHAPTER VI.
DESPAIR.

"Yes, I'd rather speak in this dusk," said Sir Lewis, as the servant retired and Valerie sank once more beside him. She was trembling with delicious suspense. Her heart 'throbbing as it had never before throbbed, while in her soul an angel's voice seemed to sing of joy unutterable by mortal tongue. It was a moment to live up to, for she was being wafted beyond all lesser joys of life. Her lover was about to tell her the thing which every fibre within her yearned to hear. , "You are cold, my dear friend," he said as he placed his hand on hers. "No,' no, I am not cold. Tell me what you have to say, Lewis, I am listening." She clasped his hand and held it firmly between both of hers. She was too hungry to play any coy woman's tricks. He had kept her too long on tenter-hooks. He 'must speak now and end all un- certainty. Her heart must be satisfied to-night, or she felt she must perish. It was the one supreme moment of her life; the moment which would make her his slave for ever and bid her best instincts blossom out into bene- volent and gracious deeds, or else plunge her into hell. , Sir Lewis Eastlake was, and had always been, a reckless, easy-going young man. He had made ducks and drakes of his paternal estates, and of his best friends. He thought he had set his back on all his former rashness, and meant now to turn over a new leaf and begin life earnestly and straight, but he didn't know what he was about to do now, and that must be his excuse. "Valerie, I know that you are my friend, and I think you like me just a little." "Like you a little, Lewis? Oh!" She almost sobbed that "Oh!" as she pressed his hand closer between hers. He felt the mesmeric thrill that passed from her over him, but, like the obtuse young Englishman he was, it did not enlighten him. He went on in a clearer voice, as one resolved to get over an unpleasant duty. "I told you in my last letter that I was badly hit in money matters, but I did not quite know at the time that I was a ruined man." "What does that matter, Lewis, now? Go on."

"Everything to me, my dear Valerie, for I am a beggar." "Again I fay, what matter? You can marry, and your wife will make you rich." "No she cannot, for she is about as poor as I am." "What ? " The exclamation brc4l# from her shrill, sharp and discordant. 414, He had blurted it out at last. The rest would be easy for him, he thought. The hands which clasped his tightened, for an instant, so fiercely that he winced, then all at once they relaxed while Valerie fell inertly acainst

mm. Two rapicl heart-beats was all tne time this kindly stroke of oblivion lasted, yet she seemed to have been dead for centuries. So brief a space had it been that her companion. engrossed in his own embarrassment, never notioed that she had lost consciousness, neither did he feel the dead weight which, for the two seconds, pressed so heavily against his arm. He was contemplating the wording of his story, and suffering dreadful awkwardness in the gathering of it together. Not that he was at all ashamed or repentant of the part he had played. Neither did he believe that the Duchess meant more than a passing flirtation by her attentions to him ; yet there were features about the affair which made him decidedly uncomfortable. It is not easy for a man to tell a woman who has shewn some preference for him, even although nothing serious is meant, that he has married another within the past fortnight or three weeks. There is a sneaking feeling that he has wronged the woman somehow beside him, and that she has cause to accuse him of trifling with her. Also, although this was not his fault, he began to feel that his brother-inAlaw ought to have informed the Duchess that Hope was his wife when he suggested her as his nurse. He was blaming himself for having delayed the declaration so long; clearly he ought to have introduced the ladies properly the first moment they met. It was a mean and humiliating crisis he was facing now—a deception that he was trying to explain. As for Valerie, that momentary surcease had altered her whole nature. Her heart no longer throbbed tumultuously but lay cold and dead in her bosom. An icy calm also rested upon her brain. She could not quite grasp yet the full import of his words, for a dull torpor was holding her passions and senses, yet she was able to hear and partly understand what he said. It seemed as if she had been reborn and was listening to a past Sir Lewis, speaking, with measured words, to the corpse of a long since slaughtered Valerie. That this Valerie had been bitterly deceived, whether by herself or some one else, she understood clearly enough. Singularly also this knowledge awoke neither passion, indignation, nor hatred, as yet, only wondering curiosity to learn the whole details before she could leave his side. A dull numbness, almost like peace, was on her as she sat touching him and listening silently, the numb- ness that first follows a mortal stab, before the knife has been withdrawn.

"You will forgive me, Valerie, my friend, for not telling you about this sooner, but as events hap- pened, it was not easy to do so," he began awk- wardly. "Yes, yes, Lewis ; tell me all about it." Her voice sounded low and thickly, and she uttered the words with some difficulty. "It was in this way. Hope and I have been engaged for ever so long. I meant to marry her as soon as I had seen a little life, but I plunged much deeper into the vortex than I expected. The end came and I was ruined through those 'confounded money-lenders. "Only one thing was left me: I had insured my life heavily before I lost all. Then came that quarrel at the club, and the challenge. I was desperate and low-spirited and seemed to have a presentiment that I should be killed, so as Hope was by no means independent, I thought it would benefit her if I married her before I met my man."
The business faculties of the Duchess remained clear, if her other senses were stunned, for she replied quickly: "No insurance company would rpay for a death of this kind."

"I did not think of that at the time • I purchased a special license before leaving that day for Chei- bourg, and persuaded Hope to marry me that same evening at the British Consul's house." "Did her brother know of this? " "Yes; he was one of the witnesses." "Ah, and who else?" "Only the housekeeper of Dr. Waldred." He was not a little gratified to find her his confession so coolly. "Why did you not take my cousin into your con- ficlenc,e ? "

_ He did not answer; the real reason he could not have explained to her, that his respect, as far as women were concerned, for Eric, was not as great as his liking for him and faith as regards othcr matters. Valerie did not repeat her question. "Then you are undoubtedly married, and to the —lady I thought was only your nurse: Excuse me saying more about it now, as it is too late to advise. I shall think it over best by myself. Ring for lights after I have gone." She rose, and glided from him through the dark- ness. He hardly knew she had left him until he heard the rustle of her dress at the other end of the room.
"All!" he sighed with relief. "That is over at last, thank Heaven, and Hope was wrong to fancy Valerie cared any more for me than as an ordinary friend."

Half his troubles were removed now that the Duchess knew:about his latest plunge. The money was still to be raised to give him a fresh start in life, but on that matter he would consult with his brother-in-law, and let him decide. _ .

_ He drew a cigarette from his case, and lighting it, strolled out to the terrace, to pick up an appetite for dinner. It was a mild night for that time of the year, and if Nature was dying, she was dying gently. The teira-m was carpeted with fallen leaves, but the trees were not yet denuded, and a fresh smell of newly-turned earth pervaded the cool air. He dined that night alone, as her grace sent him word that she was not well, and begged to be excused. After dinner he wrote to his wife and informed her about his interview, and how quietly it had terminated. Then he went off to bed, to think before he fell asleep, where' the name was to come from to 'back what he resorved would be his last bill.

Sir Lewis, if a thoughtless, was not altogether a selfish fellow; indeed, it was the utter lack of self- conceit that rendered him so obtuse on this occasion. He never before had known what it was to face poverty. He had always been able to fill his purse when he wanted money, and those sacrifices which he made on paper had never, until now, come so close as to be too unpleasant., What he might yet have to endure was unknown, and therefore unfelt at present. .• As long .as tht apprentice to poverty has some gold in his pocket, the best of meat, drink and tobacco to.partake of and a superfluous wardrobe to select from, he is apt to look with but languid interest on the waiting and hungry wolf. Like the young bears, all Sir Lewis's troubles lay before him. He was unable to understand the wrong he had done to that weak, loving girl at Cherbourg, and; Nature had not given ,him the instinct to know what he had done to Valerie. -* The Duchess crept noiselessly to her chamber, and after dismissing her maid, with •a gentleness which greatly astonished that personage, she locked herself in. Her training had been that of an English lady, but the blood that now lay stagnant at her heart was Eastern, and she instinctively did what her fore-mothers, the daughters of Jerusalem must have done in their hour of degolation. She crouched down upon the carpet and let her long black tresses fall about her like an inkrpall. Hours passed, and still she sat motionless and buried beneath that black cloud; her hands clasped over her drawn-up knees, and her chin resting upon them. For a time the fire light played fitfully over that shapeless form, until it gradually died out and left the room in utter darkness. For long hours, before her burning eyeballs the words which Sir Lewis had told her shone like letters of fire, that were eating into her dazed brain and searing all other sensations. Then slowly consciousness woke up, the consciousness that her lover had been decoyed from her by that pale-faced rival whom she had despised. The night was almost spent before this conscious- ness came, but when it did, her heart began to glow again, and as the heated blood surged into her seared brain, she began to think and plot. Her mad love for the man still remained, for she was of a race, on the mother's side, that never relinquished a desire until it was gratified. It a; no longer the fresh and innocent love of yesterday, however, that had prompted her to generous thoughts, but a devouring flame, fed by the most savage hatred towards those who had robbed her of him. The crafty and patient guile of that Oriental race that now dominated her, leapt into full force in these last hours of her vigil. Round and round in circles her mind flew like a vulture about its victim, now soaring wide, now circling closer as she watched and brooded upon her revenge. At last she sprang to her feet and flung the ahmuding hair from her face with a wild, exultant cry. What a demoniac face that was which the morning light fell upon as she drew up the blind. Grey as that of a corpse with baleful, gifttering eyes. "I have it! Stephen Belwood must come and induce the brother-in-law of Lewis to back that bill ; then let Lewis go where he wants meantime, until I have accomplished the ruin of those who have stolen my most precious treasure. I shall drive them to starvation, to shame and death, even though it cost half my fortune to dp this. AIL

Idewis, you snail De mine yet, even attnougn I flaw° to wait some time longer for my prize." She hastily disrobed herself, and pouring oat some chloral into `a glass, she drank, and then lying down, soon fell into a deep sletp. It was late in the afternoon befoie she appeara to her guest, and if there were some dark shadows under her eyes, this did not detract greatly from her exquisite loveliness. Her manner was kind, caressing and sisterly, and she encouraged him to speak all about himself and his young bride. The clumsy fellow was delighted at this sympathy, and opened his heart freely to her inspection. "I am glad you have confided in me, Lewis, at last, for now I can act like a sister to you and to —your wife." He had told her about the money-lenders and his intentions respecting going to North America. "Yes, there is every prospect of success, in those regions if you go well provided; and since you will not let me be your banker, you cannot prevent me from using my influence to getting you a post as superintendent for one of the companies which are forming. Meantime, as you must still keep yourself quiet, best remain here for the winter at Falaise, with Lady Eastlake, while you make your preparations, and also send for your money-lender to come here. I shall go to Italy, so that you may be entire master here, while you remain." It was a most generous offer, which Sir Lewis accepted after a protest. He could not well refuse either, even although he was eager to begin these arrangements at once, when she asked just to let her have two or three more days with him at Falaise for the sake of old friendship, before he commenced his new life.

Ah, those three last days, when this woman, young, beautiful and now utterly unscrupulous, put forth all her wily arts to fascinate him and make his heart a traitor to duty. She feigned the role of a. sister, and claimed all sister's privileges. She was bold, tender and insidious; full of inventions to amuse and interest him as only such a woman could be. As a sister she could now stroke his hair, kiss him, lean over him and against him, indulge in a thousand artlessly artful tricks that were trivial in themselves yet alluring and deadly; she shewed him her love and her regret so plainly now, that he wondered he had not guessed it before; then she forgave him his blindness with such sweet abandon that his lrad and heart throbbed with fever. Yet through all this he was true to his wife, or thought he was; but when the Duchess drove away with a last tearful and despairing embrace, he felt like a guilty cur. The poison of those melting and flashing dark eyes rankled in his heart all through that winter, and for many a day afterwards. Yet he tried to console himself with the thought that his love was still the same for gentle Hope, and that he had been staunch and true to her.
(To be continued.)
TIIE lAAIVEINER, FRIDAY, JULY 28, 1899

div.head: WATCHMAN'S NIGHT.
div.p: THE WATCHMAN'S NIGHT.

ME. HENRY WIGGIN, the Vestry night watchman, the hero of the following true story. resides at 2, klartland- grove, Chalk Farm, London, where a "St. Panerae Gazette" representative found him one Saturday after— noon. Briefly put, his statement amoUnts to this : "For cieht-and-twenty years (I am now 58) I have suffered from asthma, bronchitis, and iridigestion, and for the last ten years very severely. I tried all sorts of remedies until I was tired. I have been tinder more than one doctor's treatment, and One, a very eminent medical man, but the last two or three years were almbst too much for me, particularly as I was 60 constantly exposed to the weather. I felt un“:10al to my work ; I could not eat anything and enjoy it ; I had no energy ; the least exertion overcame me ; and I was in the depths of despair. Whatever focal was put before me, I felt 1 could not eat it. I lost my breath, and my work fairly knocked me up." •• And now. Mr. Wiggin "Now I laugh at th& work and at the way it used to affect me. And Gat well ? I should just think I do! Why, a half-pou::d of steak, that would have simply frighteued me before, I can pelish off now with no trouble, and perhaps help myself to a bit more. rasher and a couple of eggs, that would have sent me away from the table at the morn sight, I now enj4y." EXPERIMENTAL AGRICULTURAL WORK.

The annual report of the work carried out in connece Mon with the Technical Instruction Committee of the Cheshire County Council, was issued on Saturday. The amounts received under the Local Taxation (Customs and Excise) Act, have shown an increase every quarter, and this has enabled the committee to steadily increase its. grants to the various districts, to provide for eaten- sioas of work in new directions, and give greater assis- tance to the secondary schoOlsinthe county. The Count!! Dairy Institute at Worleston has been doing gcod work in practical dairying. Though the institute has been kept well filled with students, still it is felt that the farmers and cottagers do not take full advantage of the instruction there given as its importance demands. Farmen astart that they cannot spare their daughters, that labour is scarce, and every hand is required at home. The claims ot labour, say the committee, are al- lowed to supersede the claims ot education. In some circumstances this could probably be understood ; but when the instruetion is bearing upon the manufacture °Lan article upon wbick the livelihood denends,such an excuse, is, to say the least, short-sighted—penny wise and pound foolieh. All are agreed. adds the report,thaC fine Cheshire cheese requires great skill in its manipu- lation ; all are equally agreed that the want of that skill produces an article second-rate, or third-rate,wnich Igluts the market, brings down the prices, and tends to ruin the reputation of Cheshire cheese,and enhances tbe sale of foreign makes. Cheshire being 'surrounded bY so many large and rapidly-increasing towns, the growth of the new milk trade is very great. Year by year more farmers are drawn into the practice of selling their milk. Though this decreased the number of Wolf where cheese is being !nide, there was evidence to show that farmers had so improved their bolding, that a greater quantity of stock can be maintained, while the improved methods of selecting stock and feeding have materially increased the yield of milk. The report deals with the experimental test work with regard tO tuberculcsis in cattle. The Technical Instruction Coale mittee, recognisiiig the great importance of obtaining reliable information in regard to the prevalence of tuber • culeeis in cattle and the methods of detecting the prer ence 01 the disease set aside a sum of £2OO, to te, available for carrying on a series of tests and expert" ments in regard to this disease, and providing inforuir ti n which should be of value to the farmers of the c untv and the country at large. A special committee was appointed to deal with the question, and the test!' were directed to show the extent of the prevalence e'e tub ,renlous dieease in the dairy. herds • the reliability 0 the tuberculin test for diagnosing the disease eon!! idea of the \mount of loss that would be experienaed ; etearine the herds of affected cows ; and whether re: peat/el injections of tuberculin have any curative effet: in Tigard to animals affected. The experiments are 013; yet completed ; but the herds at the Dairy School stir the Agricuiturai College have been cleared of tuberol; one animals and their places supplied by others 07 hare stood the tes,. At the Agrieultural College exeerei mental tests wore made with 120 different varietiee poteoes, testing their growth with various manure.; a hoe! and cut sets. &c. A number of German variel!to were also testi d. Experiments are also being made v7l" grass plots, root and grain crop, &a.

EVEN if we could see ourselves as others see us, most of us wouldn't stop to look. THE surest thing about first love is that it is not likely to be the last. TIRED AND HUNGRY HUSBAND: "Why is dinner late again, Julia? It is half-past seven and there are no signs of it." Wife : " Well, dear, the fish did not come till seven, and the cook has the neuralgia, and the Browns never dine till eight, and I'm sure we're as good as they, any day." MAMMA,: "Johnny, did you learn anything good at Sunday-school this morning." Johnny: " es, indeed. I learned that Tommy Martin had give Benny Bellows an awful lickin'—sumthin' he's needed for a long time." COT7NTRY clergyman nailing creeper to wall in his garden when small boy stops to watch him. Shall I drive him away?" Lawyer : " His life is insured in your favour, isn't it ?" " VeP ; I made him do that before we married." " Veil don't drive him off. He'll die quicker where he is."

AN UP • TO- DATE BURGLAR.—" Safe at last." The electricity-working-up- to. date-1897 model- burglar smiled and sighed a big sigh of relief. "It was a close shave"— He wiped his forehead wearily. "But at last the reporters have, dropped the case and the police have taken it up. Now I can rest easily." OPEN TO SELL.—City Man: "Yes, I flatter my- self I have one of the finest suburban homes you ever saw." His Friend: "Is that so? I'm think- ing of buying a suburban place myself." City Man: " Really ? Buy mine !' PARSON: "George you haven't been to church very lately. Why not?" George: " Noa oi ain't, parson an' wot's more, sir, oi hopes no offence, but oi reckon that a man as gives the first prize at the flower show oot o' his own parish ain't no fit minister of the gospel." REMARKABLE GROWTH. Housekeeper; "It's queer that the potatoes you bring should be so much bigger on the top of the basket than they are at the bottom." Grocer: " P'taters, ma'am, is growin' so fast now thet by the time I git a basketful dug the last ones is ever so much bigger than the fust ones." A THING TO BOAST OF.—Two men who had been at school together when they were boys met, and talked of old times. "By the way," said one, "I saw Smith when I was out at Seattle." "Did you? And what was he bragging about when you saw him?" "He was bragging about his modesty just at that moment." Dear old Smith ! Just like him!"

BOUND TO DINE.—" 1 thought I'd just drop in, dear boy, knowing that you were having a fevg friends to dinner, and hearing that there were just thirteen. You know your wife is so superstitious about that number." "Quite a mistake, my dear fellow; we are just twelve." Well, I'll stay any- how, if only to laugh your wife out of her whim." HORSES NOT WANTED. A horse-dealer in Nebraska wrote to a friend in Washington to ask if there was a good chance for him to sell hie horses in that city, and received the following reply :—"Dear —, —lt's of no use. The people here ride on bicycles; the tramcars here are worked by electricity ; and at the Government offines they employ donkeys. Therefore, of course, no horses are wantocl."

"No sir ! You shan't kiss me! Don't you touch me ! If you do, Pll scream !" " Why, Dollie, what's the matter?" " You know well enough what's the matter ! Didn't I hear you tell Dr. Fourthly not five minutes ago that you had always been deeply interested in Joan of Arc? You false, faii hles3 man ! Before we were married you—you told nn) was the—the only woman in all the world you had ever—ever bestowed a single thought upon? B-hoo ;" Wiry HE LEFT. —A boy calls on a farmer to ask for a new place. Farmer: "Do you know anything about norses ?" Boy : " Yea, dun nowt else all my bile." Farmer: "Why did you leave your laet place?" Boy (with much feeling): "Ah !" Farmer: "That's no answer. Why did you leave ?" Boy: "Well, if you mun know, you moo knew. Furst 'twas old cow died, and we hail to eat she ! " Farmer: " Well, what next?" Boy 'Then old sow died, and us had to clai she ! " Farmer: "Still, I don't see why you left." Buy : "Don't ver then? Whoy, then the old inieeue'died--- and I bolted !" NOT LIR: ELY. —A worthy canon, who had been de.ipieased by his gardener, sought an interview witie tee offender in order to reprimand him. Knowing that if he was able to avoid the inter- view until his master's wrath had abated he would come off more easily, the man kept out of his way. A few days afterwards, however, when the storm was quire over, master and man came face to face in one o the hothouses, and the canon asked: "Why have you avoided me in so pointed a man- ner of late, .Johnson?" To which the gardener replied : " Now I'll put it to you as a man, sir : Would you, if you could help it, stand in front of a canon to he blown up?" HIS MEDALS—The cemmanding officer of a Yorkshire yeomanry regiment was congratulating the "A" troop on its appearance, and referred proudly to the medals worn by some army veterans in the ranks. Private Harvey went home that night in a thoughtful mood, and next morning he came on parade with several medals on his chest. Sergeant: "I didn't know you had been in the reula.rs." Harvey : "No, I ain't." Ser- geant: "What about the medals, then • they can't he yours?" Harvey: "Can't they, indeed. But they be. My old coo won 'em all at Otley Show." A COLOUR. Seeteme.--Wanderer (returned after Eev,ral )ears) " Well, well, I'm mighty glad to see you. How are you, and how are all the good people?" Stiyathoine "Oh, we're all right, and go-ring along as well as could be expected." Wanderer: "And how is the widow Green?" Stityathorne : "She isn't so Green as she was." Wanderer: " What's the matter? She isn't grey, I hope." Stayathome : "No; she's Brown." Wanderer: "Brown?" Stayathome : "Yes. Married Samuel J. about five years ago, and she's been the widow Brown for the last two years or such a matter." Wanderer: "You don't say Stayattiome: "Yes." Wanderer: "Well, by gosh, if she's willing to change colour again, I'll ask her, as sure's my name's Black."

WARRINGTON ODDFELLOWS' PICNIC.

VISIT TO CHESTER AND HAWARDEN. Several of the prineipel offieere of the Conititution Lodge of the ladependeet Order of Oddellows (Man- chester Unity), accompanied by the C.S. of the district (Bro. John Emsou) and a few members of other lodges had a picnic to Chester and Hawarden on Satur- day. They left Bank Qui,' Station at 1.1.8 p.m., Chester beine reached ire good time Taking train horn the Che.ster Great Central the party arrived at Hawarden abut three o'clock. Rain was falling heavily, and continued to do se during the greater part of their et .y, much to the party's discomfort. Despite the unfevour die weather they visited the places of in- terest in the village, chief among which were Hawarden Castle and the church. Tea at the Glynne Arms Hotel was heartily enj eyed, and the return journey was com- menced shortly after eiv o'clock. Arrived at Chester a visit was made to the Victoria Lodge of Oddfellowa, held at the Oddiell)ws' Hall, in Levier Bridge-street, where the Warringtou brethren were heartily welcomed by the members. Bro. TnOlleAS MILLS, P.P.G.M.,the C.S. of the district, who had recently had the honour of being elected on the directorate of the Order, welcomed the visitors, and spoke of the good feeling that had in past years existed between the Warrington and Chester districts, and the many pleasant and friendv visits that had been made by one district to the other. He hoped those pleasant memories would be revived, and had pleasure in propos- ing the health of the Warrington brethren, coupliag with it the name of Prey. C.S. John Raison. Bro. Eetsoet said it was a great 'pleasure to him to visit the Victoria Lodge. He had often bee° present at their meetines in his official capacity, and more often in his private capacity. He would take that, his first opportunity of offering to Bro. Mills and the Ctiester district, his hearty congratulations on the honour that had been conferred by his appointment on the Board of Directors. (Hear, hear). L.G.M. ALBERT SMITHSON thanked them for the hearty welcome they had extended to the mernLers of the Constitution Lodge. Referring to Bro: Mills he thougbt, from what little he knew of him, that he was the right men it, the right place on the Directorate, and they would watch with interest his career on the Board, which they all hoped would be a succeisful and useful one. (Applause.) He regretted that some of their party had had to leave the city earlier, and were thus unable to be present at the meeting, but he was sure that those who had stayed would remember that, taeir first visit, with pleasure. P.G. THOMAS S. STEELE also thanked the members for their kindness, and invited them to pay a return visit to the Constitution Lodge at Warrington, which was the mother ledge of the district. He could assure them that when they did so they would be right loyally received, and would be as heartily welcomed as they had been at Chester. If it ahould prove inconvenient to pay a visit to the Cousti- tution Lodge, which was held on a Saturday evening fertnightly, he was sure the members of the Admiral Nelson Lodge would be delighted to see them at Warring- ton on the 18th September, which was a Monday, when they intended to present C,S. Emion with an illumin- ated address in recogni ion of 25 years' faithful and de- voted services as secretary of the lodge. (Hear, bear.) Whichever lodge they visited they would be equally welcomed. In ,conclusion, he proposed health and suc- cess to the Victoria Lodge, coupling with it the name of the Noble Grand.

Mr, G. CROSBY, in returning thanks, accentei, on be- half of the lodge, the kind invitation of P. G. Steel, and promised thtt arrangements should be made for a re- turn visit to Warrington in the near future (Ap- plause). A song having been given by P.G. Fred Lvigh (War- rington), and a recitation by P.P.G.M. P. Mills, the visitors had to leave to catch the train t) Warrington, which was safely reached shortly after ten o'clock.
THE HUMOURS OF SCOTCH PREA.CHING,

"A Scotch parson, in the great Rebellion, said in his canting prayer, • Lord bleis the Grand COUGeil, the Parliament. and grant that they may all hang together.' A country fellow, stardiog by, said, ‘Amen,with all my heart, the sooner the better; and l'm sure ',tis the prayer of all good people.' Friends,' says the parson,' I dont mean as that fellow means ; but pray that they may all hang together in accord and concord." No matter what cord,' answered the rustic, `so 'tis a strong cord.' " In such a country as Scotland, where preaching is so very highly esteemed, there must be diversity of style in pulpit eloquence. In the lawland part of Perthshire there was, " some years ago," a minister of such vocal powers" that when he pronounced the word Cappadocia the women began to sob, and when he brought out illesopotamia there was a general concert of affliction." In the island of Sands, in Or:xney, ' the clergyman of one of the churches was accustomed to pray, during stormy weather, that, as there were likely to he so many shipwrecks. God would think on them, and send some to the poor island of Sanda."That w,rs very ineffectual preaching which was addresse I to a gentleman on board when the ferry- boat between L?ith and Kinghorn was in great danger. He was advised to tru.t in Providence. 'So I do,' says he ; ' but if once I get on shore I shall not trouble Him again so long as the brig of Stirling lasts.' Of two rival candidates for one pulpit the following story is told. At a church in Scotland where there was a popular ' call for a minister,' as it is termed, two candi- dates offered to preach, whwe names wrrs Adam and Low. The latter preached in the morning, and took for his text, Adam, where art thou ?' He mad, a very excellent discourse, and the congregation was =eh edified: In the afternoon Mr, Adam preached upon these words : ' Lew, here am I.' The impromntu and tha sermon gained him the appointment."—From " Ira' Auld Lany" Stine, in the " Cornhill illayazine " for August.

After the other busintss (which was of the usual character) had been completed the lodge closed in he usual way.

div.head: WARRINGTON CLERGY INSTITUTIONS. ANNIVERSARY AND MEETING OF SUBSC RIBE RS.
div.p: WARRINGTON CLERGY INSTITUTIONS. ANNIVERSARY AND MEETING OF SUBSC RIBE RS.

The anniversary of the Warrington institutions of Cler,- y Widows' and Orphan,' and the Clergy Daughters' School was held at tile Training College at Warrington on Wednesday. The proceedings commenced in the morning with a meeting of the subscribers. The President for the year, Sir Francis Powell, M.P., was unable to he present owing to Parliamentary duties, and the Dean of Manchester was voted to the chair. There were also present: —Archrleacon Gore, Revs. J. H. Carson, Canon Greenall, Canon Bethel Jones, Symonds, Canon Williak, Canon Willis, Canon Penrhyn, E. C. E. Carleton, H. Harry, Wilcockson. Canon Spooner, Mr. Fullagar, Dr. Watkins, Mr. .J Tinsley, Mr. John White and Mr. J. W. C. Haldane (Liverpool). ; n addition to a communication from the President, apologies were sent for non-attendance by the Dean of Chester and the Earl of Derby. CLERGY WIDOWS', AND ORPHANS' PENSION FUND.

The Rev. Canon PENRHYN in submesting the annual report said as was too often the case they had again to open the report with the record of the loss, since the last anniversary, of one of the oldest members of tlaeir_ conamitt ,e, the Earl of Lathom. Though prevented by other duties from often attending the meetings of their committee,in this case he had twice teem chosen as presi- dent for the year: as long ago as 1860,es Lord Skelmers- dale,he accepted the appointment ; again in 1884 as Earl of Lathom ha took the chair both at the annual meeting and at the luncheon. Their committee would recom- mend that Lord :Alford be Invited to take his place on the committee. Another vacancy had been occasioned by the temoval from the Diocese of Maneleester of the Rev. Honourable A. Lyttleton ; and while regretting the loss of his services here, they cordially welcomed his promotion to the Episcopate. Their committee would suggest toe name of the Rev. Canon Rogers, vicar of Sc. James', Accrington, to fill his place. No other names having been sent in to the secretaries, the retiring mem- bers as under were elected subject to the confirmation of this annual meeing :—Chester : The Revs. Canon Blackburne, and Canon Turner, Lord Egerton of Tatton, and Mr. T. H. Lyon; Manchester : Rev. Canon Stowell, Right Rev. Bishop Cramer Roberts, Mr. J Staening and Mr. W. H Neald ; Liverpool : Rev Canon Spooner Rev R G Matthew, efr R D'A Willie, and Mr. J.W. Fair. Of those of whom grants were made last year, two widows had died ; one orphan being in better circumstances had voluntarily withdrawn her application ; in two other cases in accordance with notice last year the grants cease. The amount thus liberated for other cases was £6O. On the other hand they had three new cases (widows) from Manchester and two from Liverpool ; two new cases (orphans) from Chester and three from Liverpool. The annual meeting would be asked to sanction pensions, donations, and payments for free scholars at the Clergy Daughters' School to the amount of £2,125; and if the recommendations of their committee are approved, there would be their list from Choter, 18 widows and 13 orphans ; Maecheseir, 31 widows aad 19 orphans ; Liverpool, 15 widows and 11. orphans ; and free education for six orphans : being two from Chester, two from Manchester, and two from Liverpool. rhe income for the year ended December 31st, 1898, was £2,022 173 id made up as follows : Donations, £llO 15s 2d ; interest on investments, £BO3 18s 3d ; collections, £435 7s 7d ; subscriptions £723 2s 61 ; unapproprieted funds (clergy and laymen), £100; bank interest. £29 13s 71 as against a total of £2,025 2s 6 1 for the previous year. Tbey might congratulate themselves that these figures allowed an improvement in all the chief sources of in- come, investments, collections, subscriptions, and donations, but though in the right direction, it was not any great advance ; and as the claims upon the funds were still continually increasing they must Ilene of them relax their efforts, but do their utmost to gain a further advance in their heads during this present year. The CuAtemide, in moving the adoption of the report, I said he was pleased the income was increasing. It was intended to appoint an organising secretary vibese business it would be to canvass the three dioceses with , a view to securing a larger permanent income. (Hear, hear) By the appointment of such a person, and in other ways, it was their intention to expand the institu- tion in every direction.
Dr. WATKINS seconded and the repnrt was approved.
APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT.
The appointment of a president and preacher for 1900 was held over, pending a communication from the Bishop of Manchester.
REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE OP MANAGEMENT.

The Committee of Management in presenting their annual report to the subscribers said they noted wi:h pleasure the steady increase in the number of the sche'ars. In July, 1898, there were 49 pupils,in Decem- ber 58, in March 61, and this term there had been 64. The health of the schoel had been very satisfaetory.Vari- ous examinations had been held at the schoel during the past two months. Of the Music and drawing toe reports have come. Nine papers and two honours were obtained in the former, and thirteen papers and nine honours in the latter. The results of the Cambridge Higher Local and the Oxford Local examinations would no:: 125 published till August. The report of the schoel examination just concluded by the Orford delegates would be read with intfrest and pleasure. Two matters of great importance had occupied the attention of the cemnoittee during the year, one the admission of daughters of laymen, and the other the removal of the school. As to the first an opinion was obtained from counsel that it was competent to admit daughters of the laity provided the benefits and priveleges of the school were secured to the daughters of the clergy. A subscribers' meeting was held but the majority being opposed to the proposed new departure no action wa s taken, as to the second various schemes had been pro- posed and the matter was still under consideration. A mat change had meanwhile taken place in the opinions of several, and it was now believed by many that if the funds which were necessary could be raised,the removal of the school into the country and the enlargement of the college by the occupation of its premises would be to the advantage of the scholars and to the benefit of the Church. The question of an oreanising secretary to work on behalf of the Widows and Orptians'Pension Fund and the Clergy Daughters' School in the dioceses of Chester, Manchester and Liverpool had also been under the consideration of the committee, and it was probable that soon, owing in great measure to the kinduess of some generous laymen the experiment would he tried. The committee before closing their report, desired to express their very great regret at the loss which the school had sustained during the past year in the death of Mrs. Hughes, the late matron,who for 40 years served most faithfully and efficiently the interns ts of the scholars. They have heard with pleasure of the intention of past and present pupils to commemorate her nem, and many kindnesses by the erection ef a tablet ie the Parish Church and a gift of money to her surviving sisters.

div.head: ENLARGEMENT OF TRH TRAINING COLLEGE.
div.p: THE ENLARGEMENT OF TRH TRAINING COLLEGE.

The CHAIRMAN, in moving the confirmation of the re- port. hoped they were nearer to their chief ambition, which was to remove the institution to the c,untry. They had no feeling of disparagement towards the ancient town of Warrington, bat there were two impor- tant considerations which made the change very desir- able. The first was that they were seeking in the largest interests of the Church to expand the fraining College. That was the primary consideration. The Trainin2 College needed expansion. They who took an interest in education knew that the training college was the key of the educational si,uation, and especially to from A religious point of view. It was of vital importance that the Training College st.ould be expande,l, and this was the opportunity for expansion. They never knew bow soon they might lee suck a golden opportunity. 13e had it from Mr. Aciarri, a past vice-president, that he wanld not hinder the Training Callege being enlarged. Under the presentgdministration they would be able to accomplish that, and they did not know how long such favourable conditions would hold. They knew that training colleges had been enbaged. More accom- modation was needed, and they wished to share in thi• general scheme of enlargement. They would obtain a grant from the Society for the Promotion of Christian Knowledge if they acted initime,and if with the expansion of the Training Colleye ti4ey were able to secure a larger fund for the Clergy Daughters' Institution, they would he doing the hest in the intere=t of the Church as a whole. The Clergy Daughters' School could be adopted for the purpose of enlarging the Training College, and the clergy daughters with considerable advantage could seek other premises. They were v-ry anxious that that should come to loam. For a long time they had been engaged in looking for some suitatile place. A commit- tee had been formed, and they hoped very shortly to achieve their desire.
The report Wag approved. OXFORD EXAMINER'S REPORT.

The report on the annual examination by the Oxford Local Examination Delegacy of the St. E.phin's (Clergy Daughters') School, Warrington, in scripture, Enlist language, and mathematics waa submitted. The lower classes were examined orally with a littly written work, the seniors on paper only. The examiner. Bober!. Ewing, M.A., late fellow and tutor of St. John's College. Oxford, Trowbridge, said it was the third time he hat examined the school, and he could sea steady progress each year. The report was adopted.

div.head: WARRINGTON DIVORCE CASE. A WIFE7L-SULTERY.
div.p: A WARRINGTON DIVORCE CASE. A WIFE7L-SULTERY.

In the Divorce Division last Thursday, Mr. Justice Barnes had before him the case of Robertson v. Robert- ,,,on and O'Shaughnesiy. The petition was that of Mr. James Menzies Robertson, manager of the British Work- man's public house, Horse Market-street, Warrington, for a divorce by reason of the adultery of his wife, Ester Anne, with Mr. Charles Joseph O'Shau,ghnessy. There was no defence.

Mr. Bayford, who appeared for the petitioner, said that the marriage took place at the Baptist Chapel, Nlyrtle-street, Liverpool, on the Bth April, 1884. Mr. and Mrs. Robertson afterwards lived together at Liver- pdol and various other places. In March, 1891, they took a restaurant at Liverpool. In February, 1893, the co-respondent came into their employ as a general manager, and after a time petitioner had a bad attack of influenza, and was confined to his bed. He heard that his wife had been walking out with the co-respondent, and when he taxed her with it she admit- ted it. He immediately turned the co-respondent out of the house and discharged him. He tried to get the res- pondent to leave, but she refused to go. From that time he ceased to cohabit with her,aud for three years they occupied separate rooms. In March, 1896, peti- tioner's business went wrong, and he had to compound with his creditors. After that the respondent left the house and went to live with the co-respondent, with whom she had since been residing. In April, 1895, she had a child by the co-respondent. Owing to want of means petitioner was not able at that time to take pro- ceediugs. There was a confe,sion, signed by the wife when she was at Liverpool, to the effect that she had committed adultery with O'Shau4bnessy, and that at the present time she was living with him in London. In the course of his evidence petitioner said that he was a Scotchman by birth, lie had lived in England for 27 years, and had made this country a permanent home. After the marriage he resided with his wife in Liverpool, Birkenhead. and Warrington. At to the res- taurant business in Liverpool his wife managed it and the co-respondent assisted her. When he had the influ- enza he was in bed for three weeks. He heard about his wife through his little boy. He taxed her with. walking out with Mr. O'Shaughnessy, and she admitted it, stating that she had got to love him. After he die. charged the co-respondent he hung about the door, and witness said he hit him on the side of the head. Bs. wife called out, " what a shame." She refused to leave the house, and they had since occupied separate rooms. She used to go out of a night and refused to say where she had beets. Subsequently she left him. Evidence was then given to the effect that in Loon the respondent and co-respondent lived together. ' His Lordship granted a decree nisi, with custody of the children.

div.head: FILESMITH'S STRIKE AT IN A RRINGTON.
div.p: THE FILESMITH'S STRIKE AT IN A RRINGTON.

There is no new development to record in connec- tion with this strike which has now nxtended over a period of four weeks. About two hundred men are receiving strike pay from the funds of the local association. An appeal has been issued to t'ze trades unionists of Great Britain. It runs as follows : 'We the Filesmiths,of Warrington,earneAly appeal for support to enable us to continue our struggle with the Masters, who refuse to accede in any way to our demands for a slight increase in our wages, which are practically the same as they were 50 years ago. The Trade Unionists of this country,will readily recognise, that we have serious and just cause for complaint,when we state that,atter having Qerved seven years' apprenticeship to the trade, our wages do not on the who!e exceed ..E1 per week. We can ref er,with pleasure,to the fact that we have been affiliated with the Warrington Trades and Labour Council since its inception, about, 25 years fwo., We are also incorporated with the Federated File Trades of Great Britain. You will therefore see that we have embraced the great principle of unity of action. Should any lodge or branch of Trade Unionists, or any Trades. Council, desire one or more of our members to wait upon them, for the purpose of explaining in greater detail our position, we shall be pleased to comply with such „iu,st. Roping and believing that our appeal will not he in vain, we are, yours faith f ully, JOSEPH DAGNALL, president, JAMES 13ATTERS13Y, secretary. A nuratier of subscriptions have been received in- clucing one of £5 from the Nliners' Elope, lodie, Whiston.
