div.head: EX ALMIN ,
div.p: THE EX ALMIN ,
JULY a;th 1899.

WHAT has the Conference The c onference and done to put a stop to the Armaments. enormous armaments of the Continental Powers? It has simply declared that "the limitation of the military charges which at present oppress the world is greatly to be de- ired," If we tarn to naval matters we find that the great military Powers have been anxious to restrict naval warfare, and to apply to it some of the provisions of the Geneva Convention. Indeed, &O far has this disposition been carried that some critics are already saying that to hamper Engladd has been one of the principal aims of the other Powers. It does not appear that any of the pro- visions which have been agreed to or are likely to be signed touch the great armies of the Continent. Russia has not disarmed, and neither Germany, Austria, nor France has come forward with pro- positions designed to diminish the effectiveness of their land forces. We are told, in fact, that there was never any chance that disarmament was likely to become a Practical policy. Yet half the enthusiasm created in favour of the Conference was on the assumption that it was about to bring about, if not disarma- ment, at least some arrest-of armaments. Germany soon made it clear that she would be no party to any measure of this kind., and Russia, whilst in- tent on maintaining her own enormous laud forces has been eager to impose whatever restrictions she • could upon naval operations. We do not therefore declare that the Conference has been a failure, but we do say that its successes are not of the kind which were promised when -the Czan, first opened the movement. His manifesto laid more stress upon the heavy burden of armaments than upon • anything else, and these burdens will remain. The two great successes of the Conference are the • acceptance of the principle of international arbitra- tion and the application to naval warfare of the principles of the Geneva Convention of 1:864. The other matters are of comparative ."Ittin- importance. The great armaments will all l'emain in exactly the same position as if the Con- forence had never been thought of. We venture to think that there will be eerrespon'ding dis- appointment. The situation is not one over 'Which we feel that we can display any large •artiount of enthusiasm, or listen with patience to 'the expositions of persons who have proclaimed that the Conference was to arrest armaments, and 113 now to be rejoiced over as having attained to 'aotue measure of SUCCEI3S on arbitration. Arbitra- tion is valuable, and we regard it as one of the aubetitutes for war, though it is much less likely Obe employed by or enforced upon countries saving large armies,easEy mobilised and equipped fnls,Nar. We had better moderate our hopes accordingly. The results,cannot be finally grouped Ufitil all the proceedings are over, but we believe it will take a considerable amount of sophistry to Illake the B ritish people believe that the Confer- ence has realised the er pectations originally foliaged about it. Probably, we we misled, or 'victimised by cur own genercus anticipations. As It is, the success can only be regarded as very nioderate, and he must be a sanguine man who thinks it has achieved anything likely to lighten the European situation.

THE amiable people who Is Redistribution Urgent? are anxious the Government ohould take up the difficult problem of edistribution next year are probably destined to be disappointed. No Government • takes in hand so dangerous and complex question except upon the enormous pressure of great public demand. Where is the public rand at the present tine? The constituencies "114 re not yet grown angr:ily dissatisLed with the Settlement of 18E5. There are some anomalies, is :true. Several large -towns return fewer mem- uerv. than they ought to do ; there -is a lack of BYrilect.try in several of the constituencies, and "e ortwo returning only ene or two members ght be advantageously cut up into three. Some 1_44 us aroby no means pleased with the repro3enta- 'i°4 of the Universities. But do these ttriatters form a sufficiently important case h° represent urgency? Decidedly not. We aye to look elsewhere for the motive- (l"iver of the whole movement. Certain the Unionists want to make another g hole in the Act of Union between Great , tain and Ireland. The hundred members -4zigned to the Emerald Isle are regarded as too .414% and the notion is current that it would be a `l()thtl thing to take away twenty or thirty mem- e.rs from Ireland and give them to English con- Such an arrangement would violate • Pact we made with Ireland when we destroyed Cr Parliament and brought her into our own 378 tern• It would revive the Irish glestion in its rnost acute phases. But it would do a good deal -11 ore than that, because it would bring into the

region of debate a number of questions now await- ing consideration. Is not the House of Commons too large as it is ? Does not the size of the House which prevents all members from even being pre- sent, tend to keep members away frovui it, and dis- courage efficient attention to public business ? Is it not imperative to reconsider the relations between the popular and the hereditary Chambers? If we are going to cut down the Commons, why should we not cat down the Lords? If we attack University why should we a low spiritual peers to escape? If we cut down the number of Irish M.P.'s, must we not also cut down the number of Irish peers? In other words the need for redistribution is not urgent, and the arguments for it are all on a small scale. But, if we are to make a really serious question of it, we must go far beyond the ideas of Mr. KIMBER and his friends. We hardly think the time is ripe for any general rearrangement of political power. The Liberals desire to see the House of Lords put in a more reasonable relation to the popular Chamber, without touching other matters. If, however, there is any serious intention, after the almost certain refusal of the Government to take up the subject in a limited way next session, to agitate the reform of the House of Commons at the general election, there will be a bigger impulse for a reform of the Clouse of Lords, and great constitutional changes will then become impera- tive.

The Duchess of Sutherland has set the ladies of the land an excellent example by fitting out Trent- ham Hall with pottery ware manufactured with leadless glaze. During the last twelve months a strong light has been thrown on the little-known sufferings of the Staffordshire pottery workers, due almost entirely to the contact their work brings them into with the poisonous glaze. Much sympathy has been expressed in all quarters, buL its value would be greatly enhanced if it took the practical form given to it by the Duchess of Sutherland. Excellent china can be made with leadless glaze, and still cost no more than the ordinary ware. Ladies who feel genuinely sorry for the unfortunate workers in the potteries should bear this fact in mind when next they buy pottery for the household. By insisting on having goods stamped "leadless glaze" they will be doing these poor people an immense service. If a demand can only be raiF_!ed for the safety brand of pottery,the dang- erous glaze will soon become a thing of the past, and the Duchess of Sutherland deserves great praise for having done her best to stimulate such a demand.

Ins interesting to learn that Rosicrucianism still flourishes in England--though more, appar- ently, on account of its storied past than from any probability that its original pretensions are in the way of fulfilment. An esoteric society dating back, according to tradition, two thousand years before the Christian era, it was, curiously enough, revived after the renaissance of learning, and took the form of a brotherhood. There is no record of a Rosicrucian sisterhood, or its mysteries would long since have become common property. In that respect it has gone on the lines of the Freemasons, recognising that no woman can keep a secret. Even the origin of the name is obscure, at least in its first part. The Rosa may be synonymous with the rose, so frequent in religious symbolism, or it may have a family association with the Latin word " rosa, ' dew. The former is now generally accepted and the united rose and cross make the emblem of the brotherhood. The Rosicrucians were men who claimed to have a knowledge beyond any curriculum, to see with, as it were, a peculiar gift of vision behind thoGe postulates with which the different branches of science begin, and they held tenaciously, as indeed they may now, to a doctrine akin to apostolic succession. When a itosicrucian was tired of life—"resigned it by his own act" was the term, though it seems always to have been what we should call a natural death—he be- queathed the philosopher's stone and the elixir of life to the aspirant he deemed the most worthy depository of those treasures. Of course it follows that some of the order who thought well of the earth used their powers to obtain extrordinary longevity, but the rule was never to betray the possession of this force. A writer in the "Forum" says that Edward Balwer (Lord Lytton) was in his time the nominal leader of the order. The great novelist could seo that such a society had a mine of humour, and a fresh, simple way of ex- plaining things. The present organisation in Eng- land numbers one hundred and forty-four mem- bers—the square of twelve—but apparently makes no preternatural claims.

The great art of restaurant keeping is to balance as near as may be the supply and demand. A London correspondent points out that in few places is that difficulty more seriously felt than in the House of Commons. The chef requires to be a politician in order to gauge the number who will remain in the House to dine. The best calcu- lations must be regulated by the contingencies of an exciting debate, a party division, the proba- bilities of pairing, and absolute indifference to the event that is proceeding. There is always that rare occurrence, a count-out just before the dinner hour. It happenson two or three Tuesdays in the session, when these days belong to private mem- bers, and it may involve a loss to the caterer of between £lO and £5O, The story is told, on the other hand,that when one sitting W4S unduly pro- longed, cabs had to be sent round Westminster in search of food, and no fewer than 2,000 eggs were poached that dewy morning. As a matter of fact, a junior Government Whip, who is a member of the Kitchen Committee, generally rallies a mini- mum of members for dinner, and thus the extreme of loss on an ordinary dinner is avoided. Very few are the occasions that it has been found neces- sary in recent years to provide breakfasts there, but those occasions have been lively—and profit- able for the caterer.

The value and effectiveness of discipline were well exemplified in the destruction of the reforma- tory ship Clarence by fire in the Mersey. Flames broke out on the venerable three-decker at so early an heur as two o'clock on Wednesday morn- ing and within a very short time she was burning fiercely and with no hope of being saved. The 240 boys who were on board, though roused from sleep in such a startling manner, maintained an admirable coolness and respect for the orders of their superiors. Discip- line quite triumphed over all personal apprehen- sion with the result that the whole ship's company was transferred without the slightest mishap to the tugs which were berthed conveniently near. These boys are of the stuff which has made Britain's maritime -supremacy, and their actions in such a trying time prove conclusilrelv that the race of English seamen is not extina yet, the dis- placement of the sailing ship by the steam boat notwithstanding. The cause of the disaster remains shrouded in mystery, which is somewhat heightened by the fact that the Clar- ence's preiecessor, a vessel of the same name, was destroyed by incendiarism. There does not seem any suspicion of foul play this time, though of course, some malcontent or malcontents might easily have been at the bottom of it. Grenerally speaking, the boys were extremely sorry at the loss of their old home, and are reported to have thrown kisses to it as it sank before their eyes.

Therci was a good deal that was ridiculous in the resolution brought before the Wesleyan Conference by the Rev. T. Champness affirming that no Christian man should be n manufacturer or seller of intoxicating liquor, and, fortunately, the Con ference refused to accept so sweeping a declara- tion. Had it done so, Wesleyans would, not un- justly, have been looked upon as a singularly bigoted body of men. Some of us may perhaps see some inconsistency in a man who professes Christianity and yet reaps a rich harvest from the sale of intoxicating liquor, but to say that no Christian man should be

either a maker or seller of it would be exceeding the bounds of reason and common sense. There is a legitimate demand for alcoholic drink—as well as an illegitimate one—and surely the Rev. T. Champness does not require that sinners only shall be entitled to supply that demand. If he does, we should like to know how the acknowledged or proven sinners are to be procured. Such resolu- tions as this do much more harm than good. They tend to bring the cause of tentperance and tem- perance workers into disrespect and ridicule, and at the same time alienate people whose sympathies may be on the side of temperance, but who will have nothing to do with teetotalism of such a rabid form. No 'greater blunder can be made that to push the crusade against strong drink to such an extreme, and advocates of these drastic measures only defeat their own ends by introducing them. Teetotalism never will be- come universal,and temperance itself must rely for its general acceptance on a judicious education and elevation of the people—or in other and familiar words, " persuasion rather than force."

The Warrington Board of Guardians at their meeting on last week conducted an investiga- tion in public of more than usual interest. Mr. Hibbert cannot by any moans be charged with being a talkative member but on this occasion he had a little tale to unfold which caused the flood- gates of discussion to be opened wide. The burden of his complaint was that a sick pauper who had died in the Workhouse hospital was placed in the tramp ward or two nights instead of being justly treated as an invalid in the hospital. An investi- gation was at once instituted, and although the charges were proved to be unfounded, a system of treating new " arrivals " was divulged which needs a little attention. It appears that on admittance the pauper is subjected to a bath and a change of clothing prior to the doctor seeing him. This is perhaps very desirable in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, but if the rule is made too exacting and sick persons are thrust into the bath without any consideration being given to the com- plaint from which they may be suffer- ing, serious results will follow. In the case under notice tha man died of pneumonia and it perhaps does net require the foresight of a medical man to see that to subject such a patient to a bath, regardless of the fact that he may not be accustomed to it, is an nnwise procedure. It is not our duty to dictate to the House Committee what should be done, but a policy of postponing the bath until after the medical examination in cases whore illness is even suspected seems most desirable.

A far more serious question engaging the atten- tion of the Guardians at the present time is the continued increase in the number of cases of lunacy and delirium tremens. The accommoda- tion at the Workhouse is taxed to the utmost, and on the 17th ultimo the Medical Officer had to in- form the House Committee that unless the num- ber in the institution was reduced no further cases could be admitted. The Wm khouse Master called for more assistance owing to "so many vio- lent and rough cases." The members were there- fore face to face with a serious difficulty. The public lunatic asylums are completely full, and unable to receive any more patients. The new asy- lum at Winwick is far from completed, and it was therefore a question of increasing the accomoda- tion at the Workhouse or getting a private asylum to afford some relief. One patient was ultimately removed to Haydock Private Asylum, and there the matter rests for the present. The lunacy ques- tion is becoming a most serious one for the rate- payers and the continued increase of lunatics ren- ders it a question of first importance for the con- sideration of all interested in the well-being of the community.

The regulations respecting Tommy Atkins teeth have been somewhat relaxed, but before he has time to become properly grateful he learns that the authorities are concerned about his feet and intend to devote some attention to them. Now if there is one person capable of looking after his feet we should have thought that person was Tommy Atkins himself; and if he were honoured by being asked his own opinion on the matter he would probably exhibit any amount of confidence in his ability to maintain the efficiency of his "understandings" at any time. But the authorities think some- what differently and favour the appointment of regimental chiropodists to look after the foot- sore, and the possessors of bunions, corns, chil- blains, etc. We are far from doubting that such a person as the regimental chiropodist would be of service on occasion, but we question the need of him. The British Army has managed to jog along very comfortably for a few hundred years, and reap not a little glory without the assistance of a chiropodist, and it can do likewise in the future. Old campaigners know all that is worth knowing about taking care of their feet, and the knowledge they have gained on the harl road of experience is ever at the service of the "recruity"—as Kipling calls him.. Thommy Atkins will not be made any more efficient as a fighting machine by coddling and the Army authorities must be careful not to forget this fact.
BA.TTLESHIPS AND THEIR AR3IOI7R.

The process of making armour plate for battleship,' is described in detail in a well-illustrated article appearing tin the August number of the " Windsor Magazine." '" The making of armour is a very important industry, and, so far as the heavier Term; are concerned, is a monopoly of Sheffield, where the three great firms of Messrs. Cammell, Messrs. Vickers, and Messrs. Brown are engaged in it. At the present moment Messrs. .Cammell and Company have either just finished or are working on armour for some of the leigge4 ships ever built. Among them are the " Hatsuse," for the Japanese Government,a battleship of 15,240 tons,which when com- pleted. will be the largest in the world ; and for our own Navy the " Formidable," the " Implacable," and the "irresistible," all great battlrships of 15,000 tons each. These vessels will each have about 3.000 tons of armour, and the plates for belt, cesemates, berbettes, conning towers, etc., will cost upwards of £300,000 in each case. This firm has the largest output of armour in the world. and employs in one was- or another an army of 12,000 men—enough to 'furnish forth' a considerable town did they all live in one place. But only a portion of the workmen are in the armour-making Oepertments4the rest being occupied in making steel rails, locomotive and other heavy tyres, marine shafting, and no on. Messrs., Cammell have also their own coal and iron mines. A gigantic, truly imperial, enterprise this, con- ducted, if large and increasing dividends be a test, with conspicuous success. A still better criterion may be found in the fact that over two hundred ships of war of all kinds afloat to-day have been armoured from these works. The first English ironclad was the'Warriors'whose plates were 41- inches thick. As the years went othand the Power and force of the biz VIRS were increased. armour plates were made thicker and thicker, until the ' Inflexible; was coated, or rather great-coated, with 22 inches o'i iron. But it wag, of course, impossible to go on inereasiag this thickening iodefinitely—the weight of the armour threatened to be more than the ship would carry. In 1877 a forward step was made by the inven- tion ef a compeund armour by Mr. (now Sir) Alexander Wilson, the present head of the firm of Charles Gemmel! and Company, the largest armour- making establishment in the world. The new material consisted of a facing of hard steel, with a beekine of touch wrought iron. In the present day the average thickness of most armour plates—at any rate, for belt armour—is about six inches, although plates of as much as twelve inches thickness are made for special positions. This is a vm.37 different state of things frem that which obtained in the days of the old ironelade, with their 22- inch armour. Recent improvement,' have all tended to making armour thinner, while, at the same time.a much higher degree of imneit.trab:lity to projectiles has been secured. But, for all that, the weight of a ship's armour is still very great, that of a fir,t-class battleship being not much less than 3,000 tons."

div.p: ACCIDENr TO A MINERAL WATER CART.

On Wednesday afternoon a horse attached to Mr. Ilankinson'J mineral water lorry bolted from the top of Greeuway-road, down Shaw-street, into Lowland's-road where in turning a sharp corner it was completely over- turned ,and the contents—hundreds of bottles of mineral and other arceted waters—were scattered all over the roadway. CAMDEN WESLEY kN CRAPEL CEO'S SERMONS.

The choir in the course of the day rendered the anthems " As the heart pants," " Hear my,Trayer "and " God be merci- ful unto me." The usual tea and sports, cricket, football, etc., were indulged in, acd an excellent tea rartaken of. rile trip was accompanied by the Rev. C. P. Bashforth, curate-in-charge, and Messrs. A. MISSION TO SEAMEN ANNIVERSARY.

Anniversary services were held at the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Mission to Seamen last Sunday and were well attended throughout. In the morning Mr. Joseph Stokes (licensed layreader) preached, and in the after- noon and evening the Rev. J. Fell, M.A., chaplain occupied the pulpit. Special hymns and music were rendered by the choir and scholars.—On Monday after- noon the annual excursion took place. Lsaving Percival- lane at 9 o'clock, the scholars amd their teachers and friends got aboard ship and sailed up the River Weaver as far as Marbury Hall. The excursion was accom- panied by the Weston Point Works Bind, and lively music was discoursed by them ea route. Arrived at the Hall, Mr. Jones, the,gardener, kindly conducted those of the party who desired through the delightful garden., and others enjoyed rambling through the large park. Later, tea was provided in picnic style in a field at An- derton and was thorougly appreciated by all. Runcorn was returned to at 9A5 p.m, Mr. Shaw, missionor,was in charge of the company,
A RUNCORN MAN °STAINS- MONEY BY FALSE PRETENCES.

Evidently Joseph Bushell, of Ruocorn, hss been read- ing the account how to work the •• bogus funeral dodge" upon the philanthropir:, hut forgot one essen- tial—the possibility of being found out—with the result that on Wednesday morning he was brought up at the Runcorn Police Court (on warrant) before Messrs. G. L. Davies ani F. Wiswall, charged with having on the 21st of July, at Preston Brook, nnlawfully gone about as a gatherer and collector of alms under certain false and fraudulent pretences.—From the evidence it appears that the facts work out as follows :—Bushell called upon Mr. W. R. Earp, C.C., tanner of Preston Brook, and unfolded to him a pathetic tale about having a dead child lying at home, and bning unable to provide the wherewithal to bury him. Mr. Esrp gave him 55., and there for a time the matter ended. However,from what afterwards came to Mr. Earp's knowledge, he communi- cated with Superintendent D. Pearson, with the result that the story as related by Bushell was fcuod to be a tissue of falsehoods. When shown up before the Bench on Wednesday, Bushell admitted his offenee,but alleged he was drunk at the time.—The magistrates were not dis- posed to excuse him, and Bushell was committed to durance vile for 14 days hard labour.
BOATMEN IMP' ICATED IN ALLEGED THEFTS OF CROCKERY.

Before Messrs. A. R. Norman (presiding), and F. Win- wall, at the Runcorn Sessions, on Monday, James Bar- low, the elder, captain of the " Britannia" ; Henry Morris, captain of the boat •' Spain" ; John Barlow, asiiistant to his father ; and James Barlow, the younger, captain of the " Canadia," all boatmen, at some time in the employ of the Anderton Company, Limited, were charged in custody with the larceny of a quantity of earthenware, on different days within the last twelve monlhs on or about the 19th of July last, from boats belonging to the Ander- ton Company. Limited, plying on the Trent and Mersey Canal.—Mr. F. A. Lake, solicitor, R•incorn, who ap- peared for the Conspany, applied for a remand to the first of August, on the grounds that the case haying taken an important turn was a matter for considerable investigation.—Superintendent D. Pear:ion stat ed, on oath, that the prisoners were arrested upon his direc- tions. He would say that since Tuesday he had been able to recover a considerable quantity of the stolen pro- perty, with the aid of his assistants, but considered that a remand was desirable.— Che prisoners were remanded bail being refused,

div.head: RUNCORN PARIAH CHURCR BIBLE CLASS.
div.p: RUNCORN PARIAH CHURCR BIBLE CLASS.

A large number of the members of Mr. W. E. Dudley's young men's clam availed themselves of the annual picnic. The programme consisted of a two day's visit to Blackpool and the party travelled from Runcorn Station to Blackpool on Tuesday evening returning from Blackpool on Thursday evening. Great interest is infused into this anneal outing and its success was fully main- tained on this occasion. Various drives were arranged to places of interest in the vicinity of B.ackpool and a good list of amusements, for which Blackpool is noted, was carefully selected by the party. Everything went off in " tip top " order, and the success was crowned by the able catering of the hostess, Miss All- man, Avondale, Reads-read.—During the stay the mem- bers took the opportunity of presenting Mr. Thomas Clare with a silver-mounted clierrywood walking stick, as a token of their respect and esteem for his work as secretary to the fund of the picnic party, a post which he has held for seven years, but has had to resign owing to his promotion to a higher office in the Sunday school.

div.head: SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT RUNCORN. _ _
div.p: SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT RUNCORN. _ _

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, William Antrobus was charged with unlawfully wounding his wife, Elizabeth Ant rebus, with a carving knife, on the 22nd Julv.—Comolainant stated that she resided with the prisoner at 54, Sewell-street. The prisoner came home at 4 o'clock on Saturday afternoon, and said" No dinner ready ?" Witness repiied " No, I have only just finished my work." Prisoner started to swear, and threw a sovereign on the table. Witness picked the coin up and put it en the mantelpiece. Prisoner went upstairs and when he came down again he picked up the sovereign. She then said " Will you give me some money to go and get your dinner ?" He knew she could not get a sovereign changed about the neighbourhood. He replied " No, I won't," and she said " very well," and he thereupon struck her on the fsce with his hand. He then tried to put her on the floor, and a struggle ensued, during which prisoner said" I'll do you, some way or another." He put her on a chair at the back of the door, reached the carving knife from the table. and having pulled her dress bodice off he cut her on the chest. She got away from him, and went for the police. He had threatened her for the last three rronths.—ln reply to the Clerk, the woman said she believed the prisoner intended to hurt her, and she would not like to live with him any more.—The Bench remanded the prisoner until Wednesday, when before Mr. G. L. Davis and Mr. F. Wiswall the charge was reduced to one of common assault.—Complainant having repeated her evidence as above, Superintendent D. Pear- son stated on Saturday the woman came to the Police station in a very exhausted condition. Upon examin- ing her ho found a scar upon her chest, which had evid- ently been inflic'ed by some sharp instrument. Mr. J. Knowles, solicitor, Widnes, who defended, submitted that " viltere seas not always on the side of woman," and in cross-examination elicited that complainant had taken up the" fender " and a " poker" to clefond her- self pgainst the husband with whom she had been hav- ing a row.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s. and 7s. costs, or one month in default.—The wife then applied for a eeparation order against her husband, bat the Bench refused to grant the application, on the ground that it wag cat a case for separation.
A RUNCORN CAPTAIN TO COMMAND THE LARGEST SHIP
AFLOAT.

It is with pride that the good old town bails the announcement that Captain J. Cameron, a native of Runcorn, and master of the White Star Line mail steamer " Teutonic," will take command of the " Oceanic." This magnificent vessel, the largest afloat, is reported to be making such rapid progress under the bands of its " outfitters " that she will tie at Liverpool on the 26tia of August, or thereabouts, taking her place in the already efficient N3W York mail service of the White Star Line.
FIRE AT DITTON.

About 5 o'clock on Monday evening W. H. Taylor, son of Henry Taylor, Sunnyside Farm, Ditton, discovered that one of his father's largest stacks of hay and about two tons of straw were on fire. The fire brigade at Widnes was summoned, and was speedily in attendance under Superintendent Carr, but their attempts to save the stack were unsuccessful. A considerable amount of damage was done, but it is covered by insurance. Superintendent Keighley and Inspector Strickland were also present with a number of policemen, and rendered great assistance. The origin of the fire is being investi- gated.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[By ..i. CORRESPONDENT.]

The election of Mr. Samuel Taylor, J.P., Rydal Mount, as president of the Runcorn Football Club, is hailed on all sides with delight. Mr. Taylor is without doubt Runcorn's most popular friend—and a good friend too—NA., notwithstanding the fact that he already holds numerous presidencies and ether eminent positions with their innumerable calls upon the purse, he is ever ready to unloose the "strings" and let his bounties flow into any deseryinz channel. Mr. Taylor, as president of the Football Club, will without doubt prove, what he generally is —"a regular brick,"—and I heartily con- gratulate the club on its acquisition.

The work of our Parish Councils is undoubtedly important, and on account of its peculiarity parish councillors have been dubbed "the watch dogs of democracy." They are marvellowlly keen scented —nothing escapes them. Let anyone breathe but softly of a "footpath." a " public well," a " pump," or a " dangerous fencing ;" and the instinct of the " P.C." is tally awakened. There is a gathering of the clan and behold! someone called to attention. Thus we read that eight persons assembled at the Parish Council meeting at Weston last Friday even- ing, with the nett result that Major Orred's agent's attention has been called to the dangerous state of the fence adjoining the Common pit. Truly Wes- tonians are well served.

Notwithstanding the fact that some attempt at renovating the drinking fountain, presented to the town by the Countess of Ellesmere,has been made, the structure still remains in anything but a satis- factory condition. The expense necessary to put the fountain in proper repair and working order is infinitesimal and it is much to bri regretted that such an ornament, as the useful piece of architec- ture may be made, should be allowed to stand as an advertisement of the supine indifference of those whose duty it is to maintain the reputation of the town.

The recent scandal in connection with the "Skip Inn" brings one fact forcibly to light—that the police authorities of Runcorn. under the energetic management of the present superintendent, are not lacking in determination to see that the law is properly carried out. No doubt,theiandlord of the "Ship Inn "was the 'victim of some duplicity on the part of those who brought upon him the punish- ment meted out for the offence laid to his charge, but the police authorities are to be congratulated on working up a "case "for conviction which admit- ted of little or no defence.

It is earnestly to be hoped that the plan recently submitted by the surveyor to the Rural District Council Committee, for the conversion of the Run- corn Common into a park and recreation ground, will not be shelved indefinitely as some schemes of a similar nature have been in the past. A project which makes for the physical betterment of the community and materially adds to the importance and beauty ot the town is surely one which should command prompt and sympathetic attention ; and the Council will be guilty of a grave dere:ection of duty if they allow a mere trifling question of cost to militate against the successful inauguration of so laudable a scheme.

What a pity the authorities of Runcorn are not a little more alert respecting sanitary matters. During the present tropical weather the stench in some parts of Runcorn has been an almost unbear- able nuisance, and complaints are made by the inhabitants that notwithstanding repeated applica- tion to the authorities for the cleansing of privies, a want of proper attention in this direction is apparent. Such a condition of things is likely at any moment to lead to an outbreak of more of those epidemics from which unfortunately Runcorn !lot infrequently suffers. A matter of this kind which concerns life and death requires urgent attention.

div.head: RUNCORN MAN'S NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING.
div.p: A RUNCORN MAN'S NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING.
THE DANGERS OF " CRA.BBING."

Children indulging in the dangerous sport they call "crabbing "—i.e., wading into different portions of the Ship Canal after crabs—do not always realise the risk they run. This was amply illustrated on Tuesday afternoon last, when a young man named Thomas Curzon was coming round an arm of the Canal near to an old disused warehouse, down locks, when he raw a little bey apparently about to sink a second time. Now, for a strong powerful fellow to watch a child sink requires a large amount of"nerve," but Curzon had no "nerve" of that kind, and although he could not himself swim,pluckily went to the rescue of the child. Then came a very distressing time for Curzon and the child, and both were soon in difficulties,though Curzon and the child were able to maintain a better struggle for life than if the little one had been (plc to itself. Soon the shouts for help brought Mr. Charles Stubbs, boatbuilder, on the scene, and that gentleman *lunging into the water,af for much exertion, brought both to the side. It was a plucky act of Curzon's to ao to the rescue of the child, and though he nearly lest hie life, no one will deny that had he hesitated, the child would have drowned before his eyes ; as it was he was ab'e to keep the child afloat for a longer period, and happily was timely rescued by Mr. Stubbs, who deserves great praise for his gallantry and rescue. We understand that the youngster, ques- tioned as to how he got into the predicament,laconically replied " Crabbing."

div.head: NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING.
div.p: NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING.

A number of children were playing near the Dal- lam Brook, Folly-lane, on Sunday afternoon, when a girl named Sarah Haines, 12 years of age,residing at 1, Back Stamford-street, fell into the brook, and, there being a considerable quantity of water, had a narrow escape from drowning. While she wns struggling in the water and was sinking for the second time, four boys, named Charles and Samuel Barlow, Sidney Hankinson and Peter Knowles, all under 16, were attracted to the spot by the screams of the other childten, and one of the brothers Bar- low jumped in to her wistance, when she fortun- ately grasped a stick which he had in his hand,and was ultimately got out in a very exhausted state. This ia looked upon as a very dangerous spot, and is much frequented by children.

div.head: SEQUEL TO THE "SPREE AT
div.p: SEQUEL TO THE "SPREE AT
THE ROOKERY."
A RUNCORN PUBLICAN FINED FOR PERMITTING DRUNKENNESS.

On Monday the chief item for attention at the Run- corn Petty Sessions, before Messrs. A. R. Norman (pre- siding) and F. Wiswall, was the prosecution of the landlord of the" Ship Inn," Runcorn, tor permitting drunkenness on his licensed premises, on the 4th of July. The special feature of the case rose from the fact that it was the sequel to the robbery of Ell from the flat "Fanny" by a man named S tmuel Ellie, who with his friends had spent a portion of his theft in "treating " at the Ship Inn, Runcorn. The facts of the case will easily be recalled. Mr. A. E. Fletcher, Northwich, appeared for the police, instructed by Superintendent D. Pearson ; and Mr. A. Aspinall Tobin (Liverpool), instructed by Mr. Joseph Burton, solicitor, Runcorn, for the defence. Mr. Fletcher, in opening his case, recapitulatec' the circumstances out of which it arose. There had been a robbery, and the police in the course of their duty had found the culprits of that robbery in such a beastly state of intoxication that one of them Samue'. Ellis, the elder, when conveyed to the police station with his son Samuel Ellis and Thomas Rudley, remained in a comatose condition almost until the following thy. Naturally the question arose of where the people get their drink, and he felt that the police would on this occasion satisfactorily show where it had been obtained. He proceeded to show that the people had been engaged in what he would call a " carousal" and commencing on the night of the 3rd of July had been taking liquor to a very large extent during that period. —Mr. Tobin strongly objected to Mr Fletcher touching upon anything exc-pt that which referred to the particular charge he was there to answer.—Mr. Fletcher observed it was desirable to have a continuity of narrative—Mr. Tobin : That may be so, and if I was aware that it would be something to my benefit I would allow you to go on; but as I am entirely in the dark I would prefer that you adhere to the specific date we are charged with permit- ting drunkenness on. The following evidence was then taken : Jane Radley, wife of Thomas Radley, 19 Heath-road, itunenrra, said that Samuel Ellis lived with her for a period of 18 or '2O years. His wife was a confirmed in- valid and could do nothing for herself. On Monday, the 3rd of July, it was a fact that Ellis had some money in his possession. She was with him at the " Ship Inn " kept by the defendant John Leyland, on that night, and 'had a glass of whisky. On Tuesday, the 4th July, they got up about 6 o'clock in the morning. Ellis. ssnior, had gone out. She found him at the bottom of the entry about 7 o'clock, coming from the direction of the town and took her te the " Ship Inn." They remain.d at the "Ship Inn "for some time. She had "two lemons "during the time they stopped there and Ellis had either beer or whisky. She could not swear how many glaesee Ellis bad. Mr. Leyland supplied the drink. The first time they visited the house they stayed about a quarter of-an-hour. They then went down the brilge to Mrs. Waterworth's (" Egerton Arms ") where they found witness's husband. They returned to the " Ship Inn" but on that 'occasion they did not stay many minutes. She thoueht that Mr. Elie, senior, had sometleiog, but could net tell its nature.—Pressed by Counsel, witness repeated she could not tell what Mr. Ellis had to drink on the second oceasion.—After they had been in the house about a quarter of an hour she suggested they should go home. At that time Ellis was very much gone in liquor, and she asked Ellis to go home• He said he would not and a man named Rafferty helped her with him. She put Ellis on to a sofa in the kitchen and aGvised him to have a sleep. The police came a little after nine. She was with Ellis some time but could not tell how long. When Ellis, junior, was in the " Ship Inn" he was sober, but when he came home he was drunk.—By Mr. Tobin: She did not know whether drink had been brought to their house. She heard so, Mrs. Bagley told her. When she was in the " Ship Inn " a second time old Ellis talked quiet enough. He was standing right enostieh. and was not disorderly in the public house. He went all at once "on getting into the air. Wineas considered there was nothing in Ellis's conduct that would lead the landlord to think he was drunk —By Mr. Fletcher: Ellis, senior, appeared 'to be drunk when be came out of the house. She did ask Mrs. Basley " would she help her with Ellis, senior. home." The landlord was not present then. She got served twice in a quarter of an hoar. Mr. Ellis paid for the drink. Mrs. Besley did treat them, but not at that time.—Recalled by the Bench : Mrs. Radley said said she had only two drinks—" small lemons "—on the occasion of each visit.

Rebecca Basley,wife of John Basley,Strineer's Court, Heath-road, said about 10 t• 8 she went for a pint of beer for her husband. She met Mrs. Radley and old Ellis, as she was going there, at that time Ellie appeared to have had a lot of drink. Afterwards she went to the "Shin Inn," a second time; it would be about 9 o'clock. Mr. Ellis then asked her what she would have and she said a " small peppermint" and Ellis said to the land- lord " give her a full 'tin." She saw a glass before ela Ellis, but did not know what he had had. Witness "stood drinks" herself, after which she assisted Ellis to go home. Mr. Leyland waa there and served them. When the people assisted old Ellis home he was in a very" bad condition." Inside the public house the man Ellis was very drunk and " his legs went from under him." She could not tell whe'her the landlord saw old Ellis or not; but he was in the bar. She saw young Ellis in the "Ship Inn" too,and he was more drunk than sober.—At this point Mr. Tobin said be would not dis- pute the fact that Ellis senior was the worse for drink on the way home. He was only answer- able for him whilst in the public house.— Continuing witness said she saw young Ellis land the old man having a row ; then shortly after the police came.—Cro,s-examined by Mr. Tobin: She first went into the Radley's house when she heard the dis- turbance, and a second time to tell Mrs. Hadley that they were quarrelling. Witness saw the younger Ellis knock his father on to the floor. and Ellis' wife was screaming in bed. It would be a little less than half-an- hour after leaving the " Ship Inn" that the row took plate. Witness knew that drink was sent for and taken into the Radley'e house. Radley sent for drink, and a quart of beer and some whiskey was brought into the bursa for the Ellie. While in the public house she dia not hear Leyland say anything. She had stood drinks to the people present, but would not stand Ellis senior anything, because she thought he had had enough. John Rafferty, on the 14th July, was also at the "Ship Inn." It would be between half-past eight and nine o'clock when he got there. He saw Ellis come in the worse for drink and Mrs.Radley said to Mrs Baslev "let us have the old man home." Mrs. Basley said she would net have anything to do with him. Mile Hadley then asked him to help her and he assisted her with old Ellis. The man was drunk or at any rate bad enough to give them a lot of trouble.—By the Bench : Mrs. Hadley asked him to assist her with Ellis because he was so drunk that the woman could not manage him by lnerself. Mrs. Baslev would not assist her at all. William Hughes, 56, Sewell-street, Runcorn. labourer, deposed to going to the Ship Inn about a quarter or twenty past six. About 7-30 old Ellis came in by him- self. and was supplied with two drinks—"wh'skies." Witness left the house about 9 o'clock, and had 4 or 5 pints. Three were paid for by himself and his mate,and the other two by Ellis. The five pints did n, t affect him. He thought Ellis had "had enough."—By Mr. Tobin: He saw young Ellis there and would swear that he was not in long. He did not notice old Ellis's legs shaking. George Carrington, police constable at Rnneorn, &- netted to going in search of Eilis, nen., at 9 30 on the 14th July. He got to the house about ten minutes to ten. He also gave evidence of both the Ellisea and Rad- ley being drunk. On examining the house they found one quart bottle of porter there. It was fall. There were no other evidences of drink in the home. The men were " beastly drunk." He saw the landlord (Mr. Leyland) about 320 and said that he was making in- quiries about the men, and he and the landlord had a conversation about the length of time Ellis was in the public-house. On the Saturday, the Bth July, ho again saw Leyland and told him he bad been instructed to tell him he would be proceeded against for permitting drunkenness. He said "You are wrong." Witness said "1 may tell you also that Ellis and his son were the twe parsons for whom you will be summoned." He said "I am very sorry ; I didn't think that young Ellis was so bad."—By Mr. Tobin : Both the Eilip's were very drunk. The conversation respecting the taking of pro- ceedines aeainst the landlord was after the case against 'Ellis, sen., had been decided.

This was the case for the police, and after an ad- journment of half an hour Mr. Tobin opened the case for the defence. Be con- tended at considerable length, that to permit drunken- ness had been held to mean " connivance," "knowledge on the part of the landlord "and also that the landlord " knowingly closed his eves to the bet." If. however, he proved his client had no knowl,dge of Ellis being drunk—and he would submit evieenne to re eve that the landlord, as soon as he noticed that Ellis was getting the worse for liquor had ordrred him to go home—then he felt he was entitled to go off scot free. 11aipp7, sub- mitted several opinions of juires, bearing upon his con- tention, Mr. Tobin took the following evidence : Jonn Leyland. licensee of the " Ship Ion." swore he was ssrving in the bar when young Ellis, the Sne, came in. It would be about eieht in the morning. Young Ellis stayed about 10 minutes. and had a pint of" pop and porter." It was his orinien that he hsd come in in his shirt sleeves from work. Young Ellis did not come in again that day. With regard to old Ellis, he re- membered he was taken away from his house a little be- fore nine, by Mrs. Radley and a man named Rafferty. Just before the man Ellis was geine out. he (witness) noticed the man was" going drunker all the time," and said to him he must S' go home." Witness was behind the bar, and Ellis was moving from the counter to a form to sit down, when he noticed he was going worse. Old Ellis was quiet, and paid for his drink. There was no disorder. There was Rething to complain of in old Ellis's conduct up to the time he said to him " you must go home." The reason he said that was because he noticed Ellis stagger when he moved from the coun- ter to a scat.—Ey Mr. Fletcher : He could not say Ellis

was sober when he came in, He (witness) thought be was fit enough to be served. Old Ellis paid for drink three times, and he (witness) was supplying drink to the people that the man under the influence of drink was standine. treat to. Witness did not hiar old Ellis say to his son that "he need not go to work that day as be would pay him his wages." He heard them saying something ati..iut Ellis winning the money on a race- horse. Ellis, senior, was not drunk when he came in bat had the appearanc2 ot being drunk. He did not see a woman receive 2s 6d from Ellis senior. Witness served a glass and half a glass to Ellis, during the hour he was in the house. He remembered the policeman coming to him, but he did not say' that young Ellis was not as bad as his father."—By Mr. Tobin ; Ellis was perfectly fit to be served upon coming in. Ellis, junior, stated that he went to the Ship Inn once on the morning in question, and stayed between five and ten minutes. He only had a pint of pop and porter to drink. whilst in the "Ship." Afterwards he went to the "Eger- ton Arms" and had a glass of whisky there. Then leav- ing the "A,gertoa Arms" he went home and had three pints of beer there. He was on the sofa when the officer came in. It was between a quarter and ten minutes to seven when he got to the "shop."—By Mr. Fletcher : „is: was not responsible for the "row"that was supposed to have taken place in the house. His father came by his injuries by falling off the sofa. The beer was fetched in the house by a "little stranger." Ile did not know who the "little stranger" was ; there was plenty of "little strangers" who would fetch beer for them (Laughter).—Mr. Fletcher: Would you trust them ? Witness : Yes. They would fetch plenty for 211—Mr Fletcher : Yes, but could you trust them with the 2-li? Witness : Oh ! I'd run the risk of losing that. (Laugh- ter.) Mr. Fletcher: Why did you stay at hocne ? Witness : I was n‘t so well.—Mr. Fletcher : 'sem you had had a "pop and porter," a glass of whisky cold,and three piuts of beer, but could not go to work because you were too ill. (Laughter.) Mr. Tobin here intimated that he would close his Case. _ _

The Bench after a blief retirement intima-ted they considend the case proved, and John Leyland would be fined 40s and cots or in default one calendar month. The license would not, however, bl endorsed.

Ffoulker, vicar of Clifton and Nottingham, brother of the bridegroom. There were four bridesmaids, Miss Margaret Baker, Miss Sibyll Baker, the Hon. The annual demonstration of the members of the Warrington Branch of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants took place on behalf of the Orphan Fund of the society:on Sunday. A pro- cession was formed in front of the Town hail, and, headed by the Borough Band (who gave their services), proceeded through the principal streets of the town to Buckley-street Chapel where a special service was conducted by Bro. J. Wrench, of IN onh- win, who preached to a large congregation. In the evening the members again met at the Town Hall and marched by way of Sankey-street, Green street, Priestley-street, Froghall-lane, Allen-street Horsemarket-street, and Sankey-street, to Friars. green Chapel, where another service was conducted by Bro. J. Wrench. At each service and on the way collections were taken in aid of the Orphan Fund and amounted to £lO Ms. Fine weather favoured the demonstration and tl,e processions were witnessed by large crowds.

div.head: SAVAGE Ass Aria. AT ORFORD.
div.p: SAVAGE Ass Aria. AT ORFORD.

Information has been given to the Police of a dastardly outrage which was perpetrated at OrtQrd on Sunday afternoon. A Winwick navvy, named John hte venso o, was out walking with his wife and two children, and when opposite to Mr. Smith's farm they were met by about half a dozen farm labourers, all of whom were more or less under the influence of drink. One of then accosted Mr. Stevenson and asked him to fight. He refused to have anything to do with the man, and the whole of them immediately attacked him, assaulting him in a most savage manner. They dragged him about la hundred yards up the road, thrashing him and kicking him about the body and face. His wife endeavoured to rescue him, but was thrust away and had her clothes torn. Her boy ran for tits I police, but before an officer could be found the ruffians had decatnped. They left Stevenson in a most pitinble condition, brui&ed and ble,iding all over the body and face. He was assisted home by his wife, and a doctor called in to attend to his injuries. Information of the outrage has been given to the police, and it is to be hoped that active measures will be taken to bring the offenders to justice.

for him to be allowed out on bail.—The Cbief Constable said he had no abjection to substantial bail.—Mendant was remandeJ, and liberated on bail, hitnsalf in £2O and two sureties of £lO each. DISORDERLY WORIEHOUSR INAIATES SENT TO GAOL.

At the Warrington Borough Podee Court on Monday before Mr. Bircnall (presiding), William Griffiths and Edward Burke, vagrants, were charged with having been disorderly in the Workhouse on Sunday naerning and also with doing damage to the extent of 41., by breaking two nindows in their cell.—Mr. Shearer, who prosecuted on behalf of the Guardians, said the men were admitted to the casual ward on Friday night. The regulation was that anyone admitted to the casual ward twice in the same month should not be diseharged until the fourth day after their admission, Sunday not count- ing. Defendants had been in the house before- within the month, and the regulation accer Ingly applid to them. They seemed, however, to reseet it, and on Sunday morning became disorderly arid broke the windows.— The workhouse p»ter gave evidence in support.— Councilor Shaw Green asked if the regulation was a usual one.—Mr. Shearer said it had been in operation some years. The Guardians ceased to enforca it st one time,tut it led former, an enormous increase in the num- ber applying for admission to the house that they were obliged to revert to it.—Griffiths said that when he applied for admission the porter said he would give him 10.rwt. of store, to livak every day and make him work until eight o'Anck at night. T'ne proper time to cease work was five o'clock. He was pet into a filthy cell and not allo Ned to wash himself. He was fully pre- panel to stop the four days had he been trelted like a Christian. He did net think he was a criminal and to be treated like a dog. Instead of allowing him into the day room on Sunday morning, they kept him in the cell like a prisoner. He then determined that if is was to be locked up in a cell he would go to the proper Alderman Blaekhurst asked if the treatm,nt was any different for men who went to the house twice in the same month.—Mr. Shearer said the only differenco was in the time of the detention. Griffiths was not put to stone-breaking. He was given oakum to pick.—The Chairman said this disorderly conduct in the house was getting too common. Prisoners would have to go to gaol for fourteen days.

THEFT FROM • WARRINGTON AUCTIONEER. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Saturday, before Messrs. S. Cnandley (in the chair), R. T. Fair. clougb, and T. Birch%ll, Edward Sauce, was charged with stealing a pair of brass scales, value 20s on the 14th July, the property of Mr. Robert Lowe.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty.—The Gelid Constable stated tnat Mr Lowe held an auction sale on the 13th inst., at 92, Bridge-street, and among the articles offered were a pair of Scabs. They were not bought, and were seen safe on the 13th, by one of Mr Lowe'e clerks.named Burrows who had occasion to go to the premises, and saw prisoner assisting a man named Plinston to load a e rt with goods that had been bought. On the 18:h of the month the scales were missed. Informa- tion was given to the police, and inquiries were made. It appeared that the prisoner went to the stables of Samuel Sutclife, greengrocer. in Richardson's-yard, taking the scales in a sack. He was given permission to leave them there. Be had the misfortune to be locked up the same day for being drunk and disorderly, and he only came out of prison on Saturday morning.— Leopold Burrows, a clerk errployed by Mr. Lowe stated that prisoner had no right to take the scales. They were in Mr. Lowe's possession. and he was responsible for them. Their value would be about 20s.— Samuel Sutcliffe, greengrocer, 4, Cropper's brew, and George Meakin. a hawker, gave evidence to the effect that prisoner brought the scales in a sack to the stables between ten and eleven o'clock in the morning on the ' 14tb.—Detective Barlow gave evidence as to the arrest of prisoner.—Prisoner pleaded be took the scales away in mistake and was going to return them.—lt was stated that someone offered to buy the scales frcm prisoner, and he accepted the cffer and received a shilling on account•—The Chief Constable remarked that prisone had been before the Court 35 times for various effences Mr. Lowe had complained about these men stealin things when helping to load the carts. —Prisoner wa sent to prison for two months with hard [ape ur. A HEARTLESS WARRINGTON FATHER. At the Warrington Police Conrt on Saturday, before Mr. Chandley (in the chair) and other magistrates, Robert Miller Graham, 111. Victoria-street, was charged on a warrant with unlawfully neglecting hie wife and two children, whereby they bad become chargeable to the common funds of the Warrington Union.—Mr. Shearer, who prosecuted on behalf of the War- rington Board of Guardians, stated that prisoner was a joiner and was in receipt of good wages, averaging £2 per week, but spent it all in drink. The neighbours were disgusted, and called Dr. Spinks into the house to examine the wife and children. The doctor, after doing so.ordered them nourishment. The wife and two of the children were now in the Workhouse Infirmary.— Frank Aukland, relieving officer, said his attention hal b-en drawn to the case and be visited the house and tcund the woman in a very weak state. There was nothing in the house to eat. There was no bed or furni- ture except an old quilt upstairs, on which the mother slept, and an old matress downstairs on which the two children slept. He called again on Friday and found there was no improvement, and he considered it advis- able to have them removed to the Workhouse. Ha ha seen the prisoner's employer, Mr Watd, about his wag& and found that his average wage was £2 per week.— Dr. Spiaks said he called at the house on Wednesday and found the woman lying on a piece of an old quilt. She was in a very low state. He ordered ber some nourishment, and on calling the next day she was a little better. He visited her again, and she told him that she felt a good deal better. She could not move about. lifer weakness was caused by lack of food.—The Prisoner: She could hive had proper food, but she would not take it.—Detective Barlow ssid be was instructed by the Chiot Constable on Thursday morning to call at the house. He went upstairs and found the woman lying on an old quilt. She was fully dressed and had not been undressed for sometime. She was chewing a piece: of an old crust. There was nothing in the house. He had never seen such a disgraceful sight.—Superiatendent Monaghan stated that he appre- hended prisoner whilst at work. He searched him and found upon him a box containing about 40 pawntickots and also a large number of photographs out of cigarette packets.—The prisoner said he had found those things. His wife bad been a very delicate woman and suffered Irons consumption. She had brought all this on herself. —Mr. Shearer stated that that was not true. The wantan did not suffer from consumption.—Mr. Fairclough (to prisoner) : Have you brought any evidence with s ou.—Prisoner : No air.—Mr. Fair- dough: Than your words are not much good. —The Chairman remarked that this was one of the worst cases which had been brought before the Court, and prisoner would be sent to gaol for one month with hard labour, without the option of a fine. When be came out of prison if there was DO improvement in his conduct he would be again brought before the court. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A LODGING-HOUSE KEEPER. At the Warrington Borough Pollee Ceutt. on Monday morning, before Mr. Birchall (in the chair), Alderman Blackhurst and Councillor Shaw Green, Arthur Caveny, lodging-house keeper, Ship-yard, was charged with in- flicting grievious bodily harm on James Barnett by kick- ing and beating him at half past three on Sunday morn- ing.--Mr. Browne appeared for the defendant —The Chief Constable asked for a remand for eight days as the man whom defendant was alleg td to have assaulted was in the Infirmary and would not be able to leave for some days. According to information given to the police,the defendant was a lodging house keepsr, and the man Barnett had been living at the house sine, the previous Tuesday with a woman whom he:represented as his wife. The woman and Barnett had a quarrel on Saturday,aod Barnett left the house. He returned later in the day and defendant's wife refu.ed him admittance. He con- tinued until a late hour in the evening to cell at tea house and demand admission. He did not appear any time to have seen deteneant Between twelve and one on Sunday morning Barne:t went to the house and commenced to knock at the window with a clothe prop .for the purpose, he saio, of wakening his wife He broke four panes of glass, and that seemed to have exasperated defendant, who got up and went down- stairs. Barnett had then gone away, and defendant proceeded to the police station to make a complaint. While he was away Barnett went bank to the house, taking with him a stone bottle, and lay down in the passage. Defendarsti n the meentime had been to the Police Station. He made a perfectly legitimate com- plaint, and was told to take proceedings on Monday. morning. He said that if he met Barnett on his way back he would break his head. Whether that was a mere empty threat or a serious iatention be did not know. Mrs. Barnett alleged that when he arrived back at the house and found prisoner lying there he said something to him about breaking the windows and Niced him on the bead and face four or five times- Bar- nett got up and manageu to get nearly to the Police ) Station, when he was met by two officers.' They immediately Welt him to the Infirmary. ; where it WaS found tbat DiS jaw was fractured, l He was detain< din the institutiou. Defendant was apprehended on Suedav mornine, and when chareed with the assault. said, "It is all right, but I didn't k ck him, lie came on me in the passage with a bott i, ee.d I flew at him."—Mr. Browne said the Chief C,. able had fairly stated the facts. He bad, however, oe.L to state that the prosecutor tried to get through the window on a third occasion, and was prevented Corn doing so. He afterwards put out the lainp. L •vas quite true thet be attacked defendant, woo hit ena back. He denied that he kicked him. Me was a ie:e. ee - able lodging-house keeper, and he (Mr. Browne) eeked

A Fitly°Lone Mum—Vara:a Jane Bate. 5, Providence Place was sudimoned for assaulting Alice Hunt, of 1, Provi dence Pluse.—The defendant who was a young girl pleaded guilty.—The complainant stated that the affair arose in con- sequence of a dispute about a bell. The defendant hit her over the breast with her fist.—The Mayor in fining the de- lendant one shilling conside-ed the case a frivolous one and it should not have come before them at all. A BOY'a DAMAO,. To OITTBUILDINGS.—WiIIiam Nogrow, a lad, residing will he mother at 6, Howley-lane. was summo,o3d at the instance of Hannah Litherland.of Da kin's- yard for having on the 11th July done wilful damage to two clos,ts and sheds, her property. -The Complainant's son Wasted that in order to get on the outbuildings the lad had climbed over a wall, six feet high. He had damaged the roofs of two closets and broken the ashpit roof completely in.—Mrs. Usher, a neighbour,gave evidence as to seeing the boy do the damage. —The defendant stated that he was going alter a ball. Two sla, es gave way and he fell through the roof into the ashpit below.—The dtfendant's mother told the magistrates that she had offered to pay the complainant five shillings which was refused. The timber, she contended, was rotten and she brought a sample for the magistrates to look at.—The magic trates fined the lad 5s including Costs. THE COMPLAINANT MISSING.—Jamee Floyd, 28. Jockey- street, was charged on a free warrant grant el by the maKii- trates, with assaulting his wife.—The Chi f Constable said tke prisoner's wife told a pitiable tale to the magistrates of a savage assault committed upon her by the prisooer, and she was granted a free warrant. She was advised not to with- draw the prosecution, but she had kept out of the way since, and the police had been un ble to find her He would apply for the prisoner to be remanded until the following day, n order that the complaimant might appear.—The magic- rates agreed to this course being taken. SaTunehay.—Before Messrs. S. Chandley (in the chair), T

_ Bimini!, and R. T. Fakelough. A BRUTAL HUSBAND.—James Floyd, 28, Jockey-street, was charged gn a warrant with having assaulted his wife. Alice Ploy& on the 15th inst.—The complainant stated that prisoner came home drunk on Saturday and assaulted her with a dolly peg, bruising her about the body and mak- iag her eye black.—The Chief Constable remarked that prisoner had be,' before the Court seven tim.s p.eviously, having been up twice for assault.—Prisoner was fined 23a and costs. Daum( AND DISORDEULY.—firorge Howard and Joseph Watson were charged with having been drunk in Bridge street at 8.15 on Saturday morning, and were fined Sc and °Alto each.—Widiam Jordan, a stranger, was charged with a similar offence and sent to gaol for? days. MlsceLLlNEous OFFENCES.—The following were dealt with for being drunic and disorderly: Thomas McEvoy, labourer, Friars'-green Model, 5s including costs; Elizabeth Wien Fleming, 2, Pillings court, 14 days' hard labour; Mary Hines, 3, Cuim's-y rd, Sc including colts; •Hlizabeth Heath, le, Colkhedge-lane, 53 and costs; WilLiam Shuffiston and Thomas Shuffieton, 1, Cheshires-yard, 105 and costs each or 14 days; Mary Kenny. Trafalgar-coart, Sc including costs.— Michael Lee was bound over in the sum of £5 and ordered to keep the peace and pay the costs for usivtg threats towards his wife on the 17th July.—Thomas Fleming, 34, Bank-street, fined lOs mad collet or 14 days for obscene language, and Lucy Stiargess, .2 Dolman's-yard, was sent to gaol for 14 days with hard labour for the same offence. DISORDERLY LADS.—Joseph Britton, 4, Orchard-street; Thomas Fairbrother, 13, Greenall-street ; and George Buckley. St, Church-street. all boys, were summoned for dis- orderly behaviour and breach so!the peace on the 15th July.— P.O Turner gave evidence to the effect that the defendants got on a 'bus whist the conductor was collecting f ares and rang the bell. They had received many coraplaints of this kind of thing.—Mr 81-chall (chairman) asked the Chief Constable if the recommendation the magistrates made SORSS time since about fixing up printed notices on 'buses had been carried out.—The Chief Constable said it had not and they had no 'salver to enforce the recommendatian.—The lads were find the costs of the summonses. A CASE WITIIDRAWN.—John Harrison, baker. 1, Winwick- road, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Winwick-road on July 19;h.—Mr. Jenkins appeared to prosecute on behalf of the police, and the defendant was re- presented by Mr. Browne. —Mr. Jenkins explained that defendant had taken out a summons against the policeman for assaulting him. The cases would be tried separately. At laal,-past eleven on Saturday night a cabman made a corn- olaint to P.O. Wright, sad the officer went with him into Winwick-stmet to assist him in obtaining the payment of his fare. While he was doing se, defendant came up. Wit nesses would tell the Bench that Mr. Harrison wa- undoubtedly tipsy. unnecessarily interfered, and made use of exceedingly, rude language. Bven- teeny be was brought to the Police Station.— At this point, it was suggested that a s Atte- ment of the case might be effected, and Mr. Browne with drew to consult with his client. Subserviently Mr. Jenkins was called out of court.—On returning Mr. Jenkins said they had arrived at a satisfa;ery solution of the matter, and he hoped it would commend itself to the Bench. He wished it, howsynr, to be distinctly understood that the palled were not afraid of their conduct aor afraid to meet any charge brought against them. They had no desire to be harsh with Mr. Harrison. and they hoped that in the future he would do his best to render the police every assists ace. He withdrew the charge.—Mr. Browne said that Mr. Harrison admitted that he had not done right in interfering between the peliceraan and the cabman and his fare. He expressed regret and with- drew the suntmo -is against tha ofileer.—Mr. Jenkins said he d'd not ask for costs—The Chairman observed that the magistrates in allowing, the case to be withdrawn heartily approved of the course taken. A MANCIDISTER Mllitr7E-Dl-:john-- Madeley. Moss.latse, Manehester, was summoned for ill-treating a horse by working it while in an unfit coedition in Winwiek-street on Monday afternoon, -.lnspector Canning. Ii.S.P.C.A., said 1:e Saw the defendant driving a brown horse, attached to a furniture van, along Winwiok-street. The animal seemed tu be going uneasily and tie stopped it and examined it. On the off side of the back, under the saddle, there was a large wound three inches long by one and a half wide. The saddle was pressing on the wound, whieh was suppurating. There was also a supparating wound on the withers. The animal was in great vain. Defendant said he had brought the animal from Manchester, and the wounds were dry when he started* Witness pointed out to him that from the nature of the wounds that could not be so. —Superintendent Monaghan and P.C. Hesp gave corroborative evidence.—Defend ant said he knew about the wound under the saddle. It Was what was called a "sitter," and the horse had had it a fort • night. When he turned out on Monday morning the wound was as dry as a board. Only last week one of his horses died. —The Inspector said the animal was in poor condition.— The Chief Constable said that defendant admitted that he had been similarly summoned, in Manchester, and the magis- trates there had ordered one of his horses to be destroyed.— The Chairman I suppose this horse is not in such a condi- tion.—The Inspector No,:sir.—A fine of 103 and co ,t 1(E1 2s 6d) was imposed. DESF.RTIOII.—Thomas Brennings was charged with being a deserter from the Bth King's Liverpool Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks, since February 61h, 1891.—A sergeant from the Barracks proved the case, and prisoner was re. mended to await an escort, the usual reward being recom. mended fur the sergeant. DIttINICEINNESS.—AIf red Guest was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on Mon- day night. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman James Fairclough (in the chair) and Messrs. 13irchall and Geddes. DRUNK Son DIsORDERLY.—Williarn Johneon in lien 0 paying a fine of 53 an I coats for being drunk and disorderly the previous day went to gaol for seven days. Ridgw.y, stationed at Preston Brook, stated that at 5.3) p m. on the date in question he saw defendant drunk at the bottom of a flour cart. He had to detain him 21 hours bsfore he was fit to go bome.—lt was his first appearance at the court, and he was fined 5s including bosts.

LAN4UAGE.—Sarah Ann Orme, 59, Nelson-street, Itunc:)rn, was summoned for using obscene language in Nelson-street, on the 13th of July.—The case was proved by Police Constable Edwards.—Superintendent Pearson sakt tbe woman h ,d been on the " spree" almost all the week.— Fined 55 and 93 6,1 costs.—Elizabe h Lloyd, liughee-court, a married woman, was also summoned for using obscene lan- guage in Flughes'-cou-t, on the 15th inst —The ease was proved by Constab!e Fry. who stated the langnage made use of was abominable. —The woman pleaded a first offence.— Fine 1 ss.

A DISORDERLY WoMAN LOOTED UP.—Sarah Hares, married womaa, was summoned for being drunk and dis- orderly in Stringer's Court, off Regent-street, on the 14th inst —P.C. rt. WiLon said, attr tetecl by a large crowd, he went down Regent-street, and found the woman very unruly in the entry. She was drunk and noisy, and also used -rery " high langua.-:e."—Fined 103 or 7 days. NovEL PLEA: GUILTY BUT NOT DRUNK.—Elizabeth Done, married woman. 15, Cartwright-street, was summoned for being dr ink and ditorierly Ile Halton-road on the 11ith just —ln answer to the Magistrates' Clerk, defendant said " She would plead guilty, but rhe was not drunk.—The ease was proved by P.C. Edwards. and defendant, having been prfiviously before the emir% was fined 5s and gs 63 costs. STREET NUISANCE.—Sors FINED FOR PLAYING FOOTBALL. —dissents Morris (13), and Thomas Hodgells ;13), were sum- moned for playing football on the Public Highway In the annoyance of pedestrians on the 14th July.—Both defendants pleaded guilty.—Police Constable Wilding stated he was on duty in Church-street, and saw the boys playing football with a n amber of other boys in Public Hall-street. They were playing with a " soft-ball "and not a proper football. He had had many complaints of the nuisance the boys created.—The defendants having nothing to say, were ad- monished by the Chairman, and let off on the payment of 45. fid. costs each.

ASS &ULT Br AN AUNT Is' BLLESMERE-SrREET.—Mary Jane Garnett, 23, Ellesmere-street, married woman, was sum- moned by her niece Sarah Barclay, 5, St. Jahn-street,single weinan, for assaulting her on the 21st July.—Defendant said she did strike the plaintiff, but that first of all toe planatiff had struck her." She retaliated —Sar.h Barclay, stated she resided at St. John-street with her father. She went to the defendant's house for her father's " lasts " which had been lent to Mrs. Garnett the previous Thursday (the day before). Mrs. Garnett came to the door. Witness asked for her father's "lasts " Defendant replied "They were not theirs." She replied " They are ours." Mrs. Garnett (who was ker snot) then struck her twice in the face. She did not strike her aunt at all.—Bertha Raw- lands, a little girl aged 9 years, gave corroborative evidence, and said she saw Mrs. Garnett strike Sarah Bar- clay.— annie Joyne, a ne'ghbour, said she heard Sarah Bar- clay and th r aunt at the door; the girl was very impudent to her aunt. Witness did not see any blows struck.—Defend- ant elected to give evidence and in the course of it admitted the assault but alleged provocation.—The Chairman observed to the defendant that as she admitted the assault she would be fined be and costs 12s 6d and adyiped her in future not to take the law into her own hands.

INOWAY-LIKE SHE CHANGED HER MlND.—Martha Alice ()rank, married woman. Cooper-street, was summoned for using threats towards Eliz Oath Atherton, whereby she was afraid of her bro.—Defendant pleaded no guilty. - Elizabeth Atherton said she was the wire of S, muel Atherton, and lived at No. 2, Cooper-street. The threats complained of were used towards her on Thursday the 2)th of July, when Mrs. Crank threatened to smash her face with the " dolly-pegs."—Mrs. Blizab th Pickerstaffe, a neigh- bour, corroborated the use of threats.—Defendant denied the use of the threats alleged.--The Bench decided that defendant had used the threats alleged, and order d her to be bound over in £5 recognlzances to keep the peace for six moths, and to pay the costs.—Defendant refused to be bound over, and was conveyed to the cells.—Later she ap- plied to be liberated saying she would be bound over; and that at the time she refused she did not understand she would have to go to prison.—She was accordingly bound over for six months.

STREET Le(TERERS.—James Crompton, Alfred Joyce and William Plant, all of Canal-street, were summoned for ob- structing the public foot way in Bridge-street on the 18th of Julv.—Crompton pleaded not guilty, but Joyce and Plant admitted the offence.—P.O. Fry tea Hied that about 11 a.m. on the 18th of the present month, in consequence of the numerous complaints received of persons loitering on the footptth in Bridge-street.and the vicinity of Delph Bridge he was on duty there in plain alit' hes and saw the 3 defendants. He was sure Crompton was there because he knew the man well and had cautioned him previously.—Orompton stated he was not there at all at the period the Constable stated. and was in his house before 11 o'clock that morning.—By the Superintendent KJ had no watch.—Alfred Joyce. aloe testified to Crompton not being present at the time the con- stable 'appeared, and said there was another man with them named" Sefton," but did net know where he resided.—The Bench fined Joyce and Plant 2s and 83 6d costs, but decided to give Crompton the benefit of the doubt. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—nartha Hayes, for being drunk and disorderly In Dutton's Court, was fined 5s and costr—Sergeant White and P.O. Fry proved the case.

A Row nr A PoTATo Fur-D.—A.(loe Hughes was summoned by Martha Hulse for assaulting and beating her on the 7th of J nly.—From the evidence submitted it would appear that the parties resided at Top-road, Five Crosses. Frodsham. They were neighbours and whilst in the potato field had a dispute eon3erning some boys coming home. From that they got to calling one another and finally to blows. Alice Hughes eventually knocking Martha Hulse (who was a much older looking woman)over a potato butt.—After giving both sides a patient he +ring the Chairman remarked it appeared to them that they were one as bad as the other and dismissed the ease.

DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES....ChStIeiI Davis, Ship-st.. Frodsham, was summoned for being drunk on licensed premises belonging to William Powell, at Frodsharn. on the 2nd July.—lie pleaded guilty.—Sergeant Clays said about quarter past nine he was in Nfain-street and saw the defend- ant there drunk. He saw him go to the Commercial Hotel and to the Red Lion and he went to him at the latter place and said he vrauld report him for being drunk on licensed premises.—Davies who offered no dofence was Hued 5s and 84 6d costs, or 14 days in default. A COSTLY ROAD-SIDE NAP.—Ricitard Oultrana, buteher. of Worley. was charged on bail with being drunk and incapable at Frodshara Lordship, on the 19th inst.—tie pleaded gullty.—P.O. Vragg, deposed to finding the defendant at a few minutes past nine !yin across the pathway. lie was drunk and incapable. The Constable asked Oultram where he came from, but with an oath he declined to tell. The man also used abusive language all the way to the Police Station.—Defenclant evilained that he had been up for two nights with some horses thst had been very ill, and had walked 17 miles. tie hid had " a little sup of ale "on the way, and sat down on tha roadside to light his pipe, but fell asleep instead.—Fined 10s.
