Douglas Jerrold was dining at some place where an unusually gritty salad was put on the table. Jerrold called the waiter, and asked: "What's this?" "Salad, sir." ,Jerrold: "No, it's a gravel walk, with a , good many weeds in it." Two young fathers met in the sidewalk as they were wheeling their babies on a pleasant Sunday morning. "The papers are making a great ado about hurseless carriages," said one man. "Yes," answered the other. "Just as if they were any- thing new 1" A NOVEL Accourr.—A firm of masons in an Irish town employ a hod-earner whose novel method of keeping account of lost time was brought to light lately by a droll circumstance. He went one evening to his employer's home with the sad intelligence that he had lost his account book. He said the pigs had got in and eaten it up. "What sort of an account did you keep?" asked his employer. "I had an empty barrel, and when I worked a whole day I put in a potato, and when half a day half a potato, and the pigs ate 'ern all entirely." "All right, old man 1" was the reply. The result was that he shot a hare, two rabbits, a jay, a cat, two pheasants (squatting), a fox, a keeper's dog, pep- pered a keeper, shot one of the beaters, and—had it not been for his servant refusing to reload his guns any further—it is hard to say what the bag would have been.

WiIAT HE WANTED.—" I think," said the local representative, as he entered the photographers studio, "that Pd better let you take these back and try it over again." "Didn't your photo- graphs please you?" asked the young woman behind the show-case. " Yes ; they pleased me first-rate." "The likeness is remarkably good," she commented, as she held one out at arm's length. "It is. If the resemblance weren't quite so strong I might have kept them for my iamily and myself to look at. We could have told the neighbours it was somebody else, and have made them believe it, but there would be no use in trying to deceive them with that photo- graph." "What is it you object to?" The surroundings." "But this is one of the most popular backgrounds in our gallery. Everybody understands that such things are only painted on canvas." "No," was the reply, everybody doesn't understand it. I wouldn't have one of those pictures get into the hands of my political opponents just before election for any money. Look where you have me. Seated on a plush arm- chair, in halls of Byzantine architecture, with a garden of palms in the background. It won't do. You must show me standing with one hand on a big geographical globe and the other waving in the air, while I tell the members of an imaginary audience what they must do if they wish to save the country." No FLAWS IN I.—Half a dozen travelling men were seated in the little station waiting for the east- bound train. First would come a blinding flash of lightning and then a deafening peal of thunder. A fearful storm was raging. "This is a scary night to be on the road,' remarked the soap agent. "I see where you are right," said the cigar man. "As I remember," he continued, "it was just such a night as this when the train struck a bad place four miles east of here, and the next instant ran off the bridge. I was the only passenger on the train to escape with his life. "When was that ?" he was asked. "Latter part of August, 1894." "I fail to recall that acci- dent," said one of the crowd. "So do I," said another. "How many did you say were killed?" asked the soap agent. "Didn't say anybody was killed,' replied the cigar man. "You didn't—eh? You said you were the only passenger who escaped with his life." " Certainly ; that's easily accounted for," explained the cigar man looking innocent. "I was the only passenger on die train. " Aha that's your game, is it?" said the soap agent. "Hold on here !" said the only one in the crowd who had not spoken up to this time, as he bustled in front of the cigar man; "you said yeu struck a bad place in the road." "We did, but got over it all right." "You did—eh? But how about running off the bridge?" "That's all right. We ran off it after we had crossed it. The story is all right boys. You can't pick any flaws in it.'

div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.

POLICE CASE. At the Earlastown Police Station on Monday morning, before Mr. J. W. Emmett, Anthony Hug lies, of Go'borne, was charged with being drank in Newton the previous night, and was fined 2s 61 and costs.—P.C. Robson supported the charge. VIADUCT INSTITUTE TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION CLASSES. The result of the examination in Magnetism and electricity, held in connection with the above classes, is as follows :—Thomas Banks, E Ist ; Harry Eclington, E Ist; George Bunting, Annie E. Jones, William H. Lawson, John Alather, J. C. Rawlings, Wm. Taylor, E 2nd. NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH CHOIR. The members of this choir had their annual pic- nic on Saturday, to Colwyn Bay. The party num- bering. 23 left Newton at 7 25, in a special saloon, and reached their destination about 10 o'clock. The weather was delightfully fine, and an hour or two were pleasantly spent in rambles on the beach, sailing and bathing. An adjournment was made for dinner, which was much enjoyed. Wagonettes were afterwards chartered. and a pleasant drive to Conway and back filled up the time before the hour for tea. Atter the afternoon meal, the re- mainder of the time was spent in the woods. Colwyn Bay was left behind at 7.18, and Earlestown was reached about 10 o'clock, the outing having been most enjoyable. The arrangements were efficiently carried through by the organist, Mr. might. lIAYDOCIE COLLIERIES EXCERSION.

The annual excursion promoted by the manage- of the Haydock Collieries for the employs took place on Saturday. This year those who accompanied the excursions had the choice of three places, viz., Blackpool, Morecambe and Llandudno, but, as might be expected,the majority chose Black- pool. The trippers were early astir, and the trains were quickly loaded and sent on their respective journeys. Whilst a very large number patronised Blackpool, still a respectable number chose More- cambe, now termed the Naples of the North, and an equally goodly portion journeyed to Llandudno. Frona the reports of those who journeyed to the three plates named,a good time was spent, and it is pleasing to record that the excursions were con- ducted throughout without a hitch or mishap. WARRINGTON DIOCESAN INSTITUTIONS.

Special sermons were preached at the Wargrave Church on Sunday in aid of tha funds cennected with the above Institutions. The morning service was conducted by the Hector, Rev. James Carson, and in the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. J. J. Langham, vicar of Padgate. The Rev. gentleman's discourse was of a meat interesting character, and his appeal in support of the funds of the Institutions was of an elequent character. He dwelt at some length upon the present position of the clergy of the Church of Englana, and gave as his reason why the laity should support the cause for which he pleaded,the extreme poverty of the clergy. He maintained that the stipends of. the majority of

- clergymen was insufficient to enable them to sup- . port the position they were expected to occupy. Some clergymen occupied an anomalous position, inasmuch as, accompanying the living to which he was inducted, there was very often a large Vicar- age or Rectory, and this residence, a clergyman was expected to maintain and keep in thorough repair out of his stipend, of perhaps £3OO per year. Not only so, but he often had a large family to maintain, and was expected to subscribe to this and that charity, and to other organisations connected with the parish of which he was clergyman. How then, he asked, could a clergyman afford to pay the necessary pre- miums for insurance for the benefit of his family. He said it was an acknowledged fact,that the num- ber of applicants for ordination had decreased year by year, and the reason given for tills iecrease was said to be the poverty of the clergy. He sa'd it was the duty of every layman to take this matter into their careful consideration, as the facts wlich he had put before them were undoubtedly a s' eliding danger to the well b-iing of the church. Be c _included by making an earnest appeal for funds in aid of the Institutions.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

SACRILEGE ax Sr. HELENS. The St. Helens police are at present investigating a case of sacrilege which has occurred there, some person having broken open two ccntribution boxes in the sanc- tuary of the Sacred Heart, at Holy Cross Church, and abstracted the contents. It appears that the rector of the mission, the Rev. Father Benson, empties the boxes Weekiy, and on Sunday afternoon, when he went to empty the boxes, he found that they had been forced open on the sides, and were empty. It is thought about Ts 6d has been taken from each box.
CYCLISTS' PARADE.

I fancy dress cycle Parade took place at S. Helens en Wednesday night in aid cf the funds of Dr. BarnardeA Homes for Waifs and Strays. The parade should have taken place last Saturday, but had to be postponed ow- ing to the inclement weather. A goodly number of gaily attired cyclists took part in the procession, which was headed by the Ravenhead St. John's Band, and started from the Young Men's Christian Association rooms Duke-street, about seven o'clock. A considerable num- ber of persons assembled in the main thoroughfares along which the cyclists passed.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT TO A_BOg.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT TO A_BOg.

On Monday a boy named Thomas Rothwell,aged eight years, the son of John Bothwell, a drayman in the em- ploy of Messrs. dreenall, Whitley and Co.. St. Helens Brewery, met with a shocking accident. It being the school holidays, the boy had accompanied his father to Orrell to deliver a load of beer. On the way back they were coming through Windle City, and while the father turred round to speak to another carter who was on the rear, it is supposed that the boy fell from the front part of the vehicle, where he had been sitting. The wheel plssed over the poor boy's-stomach, inflicting severe internal injuries. The boy was removed to a neighour- ing housl, and his injuries were attended to by Dr. Bellew, but he gradually grew worse, 'and died about two o'clock on Tuesday afternoon.
EXTR&ORDINARY FAMILY QUARREL.-A. LADY IN TNM CASE.

At. St. Helens County -Court, on Wednesday, before his Honour Judge Shand, an action was heard, in which Hen. ish Roberts, of Prescot, sued Charles Roberts, his nclo. and John Robzrts, his cousin, for damages for assault. Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the complainant. and Mr. Peace for the defend tnt. Complainant statEd that on June 17 he had been out for a walk, and spent half art hour at the Plough public-house. On his way back he had to pass his father's house. His brother Johathan was talking to a young lady named Hannan Williams, whom it was thought his cousin John would like!, to have. He b-gan to -chaff John about it, and he said hewc?uld put him one on that he would not i rub off the said it again. He did not say it again. His fattier came cut to take him away, when John ran at him and hit him over the left eye with a stone, making it bleed. He then went to tell his cousin Dinah about it i and Charles then came n, and told him to clear Out. Eta got up to leave, but he was knocked down, and remembered nothing more until next morning, when he found that the doctor was attending him. The doctor was still attending him. He had been idle live and a half weeks, aud could have earned 6s a day during that time. In reply to Mr. Peace, complainant denied that he was the aggressor. Dr. Brindle de- scribed the injuries, and said ha was alarmed about complainant's condition at first. He would not be fit for work for another month. He thought the injuries sustained must have been caused by very unf lir viol- ence. The defence was that plaintiff was the aggressor, assaulted John Roberts, and had to be ejected from ths house of Charles Roberts, during which he received the iojaries. A large number of witnesses was called, and His Honour said plaintiff was down, and hid had a terrible mauling. It was for the plaintiff to satisfy hint that be had received all these injuries as the result of violence on the part of thesa men, and he had not done so. He gave judgment for the defendant.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JULY 28, 1.99 SIR GILBERT GREENALL'S lIMPERIAL RUSSIAN NAVY. HACKNEY AND Mil srua MEN ANTiTaTERIAL. SUCCESSFUL SALTAT WALTON
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JULY 28, 1.99 SIR GILBERT GREENALL'S lIMPERIAL RUSSIAN NAVY. HACKNEY AND Mil srua MEN ANTiTaTERIAL. SUCCESSFUL SALTAT WALTON

At Walton Hall, Warrington, on Tuesday,an unre- served sale of hackneys and ponies from the stud of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., took place, the sale being conducted by Mr. W. Bainbridge, of Lancas- ter. As Sir Gilbert's stud consists of over 350 animals, it is intended to hold periedical sales to keep the number within a reasonable limit. The animals sold, which were chiefly hackneys and pony brood mares, ware of the choicest blood, though no mares were sold which did not leave produce in the stud to carry on the line of breeding. Among the horses disposed of seven were descen- dants of Danegelt, seven of Lord Darby 11, three of Sir George, whilst the foals were by Goldfinder VI., Caxton, Contest, Clevedon, Sir George 11., Sir Gibbie, and the champion pony Sir Horace. Ex- cellent prices were realised, for the buyers, who as may be expected had come from far and near, bid spiritedly particularly for the hackney class. The sensation of the day was provided by Miss Wilton, the handsome chestnut daughter of Lord Derby 11. Her peerless blood and her superb action, together with her remarkable show record, stimulated the desire for possession, and Mr. Bar- ker, of Bishop's Storcford, had to pay 440 guineas before he secured her and her raking filly foal by Goldander VI. Mr. Barker obtained the gems of the sale, for he also bought Prioress, by Bonny Boy out of Miss Wilton, a three year old filly with even lovelier action than her mother, for 330 guineas. Humph 11., by a Welsh rimy stallion, a perfectly modelled 12 hands bay, delighted the crowd, and went to Mr. Rycreft, of Bingley, for 210 guineas, whilst her dam, a well-known roan, was bought by Mr. Baxter. of Es4ix, for 120 guineas. THE NAVAL WAR GAME. [BY FRED. T. JANE.] " What does ItUS,ia want with a navy at all—she has hardly any coast and practically no trade ?" 'Dile is a common question in England, where we are apt to re- gard the Imperial Russian Navy as a direct " menace" to us. Indeed, all our big cruisers are "replies" to Russian ones ;even the French have only recently earned a "reply"—the new "mighty cruieers"destined to match the Je aline d' Arc. Yet actually Russia in her naval plans no more conteinplatee meetine us at sea than we contemplate meeting the United States. It is a possi- bility, it might happea ; but the naval pregrarnme is not governed by it in any way if Russia wars ,with us, her warring will be on the land as much as possible. It happens, however, teat there are other nations who have navies against which the Russian Fleet would be on a numerical equality, and there is no more real occasion to ask way Russia should have a fleet than to , ask why Germany should, or Sweden. Further, of Course, Russia has always in view the possibility of eventualities in which her ships would be acting against us in conjunction with one or t we other Powers. But this—though a bogey we well know in Eeglarvi—is Suite a secondary raison d'etre of the Russian Navy. Fur the Ruesians,with a reasoning ability not poseeseel by some of our politicians, recognise that unless given an overwhelming raj srity such a combination would have but a poor chance. And for this reason. Ii a combination an immense variety of different typos must necessarily be included; and the difficultities of handling a big fleet se compesed,esch admiral with his own' views on tactics, ewe side nite its; ships fitted for different tactics, are more immense than any civilian can possibly grasp. Our eight Majesties would " walk through " a fleet of a dozen hostile vessels of different nationalties, and if there were eighteen the " walking through" would probably be still easier. Every sailor understands why, the landsman must perforce accept it on faith. In addition to all this,we have a strategical advantage in position. However, le: us briefly examine the Russian Navy itself, without further regard to this particular issue. The Russian Navy is spokea of as created by Peter the Great : actially, however, the early Russians had a reputation as sailors a thousand years ago. Still, Peter was practically the King Alfred of the Russian Navy, and he performed his task with English aid : the Russian Navy is, in fine, a child of the British one. Scotsmen, in particular, had a bent for the Russian ser- vice, and there is a Russian ship called after one of them to this day. It is usual to reckon up navies by the ships and ton- nage, by a judicious manipulation of which anything whatever can be proved. It has the disedvantage of being, at the feast, a worthless system of comparison, and the amateurs' total energy of five in tare is still motes). For what it is worth these comparisons have already been made ad nauseam . I propose t) confine myself te the personnel, which is of far more account than the ships teeneselves. In action one battleship will prove pretty much like another : the difference lies with the men who do the handling. And in this handl- ing the ability of the officers and the amenability to dis- cipline of the men are the two chief things. It is cus- tomary nowadays to assert that " the battle of the future will be fought in the engine room," bat this eaten ehrase of a present agitation is chiefly nonsense, at any rate where ironcleds are concerned. The engine-room takes first place only when one aide wants to run away, and the run-away side is beaten by the mere fact of ita electing to try and " evade." Till recently Finlanders and Kurlandere constituted the bulk of the mere in cue Russian service. Now, how- ever, men from all over the Empire are male into sailors. Tne true Slav is said to have certain privileges that are denied to the other sailors, matters ef leave and so forth. On the other hand, if he is given leave in a foreign pelt he is a greatldeal more likely to Come back to the ship ; but this is a thing upon which opinions as to Cause and effect vary. On the whole, I fancy it is the genuine Russ who thinks being a sailor is more " fun." Boyish creatures are these big Russian sailors, more 33 even than our own "blues." In the drill shed at Kroastadt I noticed that the mere taking off of their overcoats seemed a joke to them, and when they marched past in fours nearly every man of them strutted a bit as he passed the " Ingliski," and then smiled broadly Co his fellow. One sees children do the same when a stranger is present. Now this to the lay reader may seem a very trivial thing to relate, but it has a very high nautical import- ance. Every naval officer knows that the boyish sailor is the man to do things with—a sailor does his best work when he treats the whole thing as a joke. " I like those chaps," an English naval officer watching some Russian bluejaceets once said. " They chuckle like ch ldren. That means they're good stuff." Russia, however, gets tier share of what we call " Queen's bad bargains." But the captain of the train- ing ship Veraii teld ins that he was fully prepared to take the went of them, and not a bit afraid of failing to make good stuff of them. "If I'm sure of my officers," tee said, " I don't trouble ale mt the men." Ile never had any difficulty about licking his men into shape, he told me, though, of ceurse,it is hard work in the case of men who had never seen the sea. Esactly how the licking into shape is done I did not hear, save that it was not by harsh measures. I mention this be- cause there is an impression that " Russian officers are awful brutes to their men." My own experience was quite the reverse, and I kept my eyes open on teis mat- ter. What I did notice was a good lest of the encourag- ing smile, and a sort of " we're all sailors " spirit. If a Russian does get into a temper he is " the very devil," they say. But it takes a deal to rouse him ; ordinarily ke is a very amiable person, prone to show a lot of con- sideration to ills interiors. The antith.sis, in fine, of the Russian of fiction. Tine drawoaclas to the Russian sailor are three : his service is short ; owing to the climate his sea-time is very cur—ailed ; and, finally, be is not primarily very intelligent. Tile firs'; two are co nb itod by as much meets and yards as possible ; the last is one of those de- fects that, properly treated, are the bast of virtues ea a sailor. Tile Russians firmly believe in masts and yards fer training purposes ; they will have none of the silly medern lid that because sail is no longer a motive power therefore its drill is useless. As every seaman knows, nothing can replace Ws training. in the winter t'ae Russian bluejackets do a geld deal of mast drill on shore. This is far from equal to the sea, bu.,; it is none the less useful. In tile drills I wet deed at Kreesterilt I was particu• larly struck by tine steadiness of the mere. These were more or less military drills ; still, if men are good at one thing they are pretty sure to be good at others. And the drills I watched were particularly good. The profession of naval officer is a very aristocratic one in Russia. The head of the Navy after the Tsar is the Grand Duke Alexis. He is the Russian Gaschen, but he is a professional one. The Gran'l Duke Alexander is else in the service. He is much younger and holds at present a captain's rank. He is not (as imperial and royal sailors are usually under the suspicion of being) a " feather-bed sailor' ; but as indefatigable an officer in the Russian service as Captaia Prince Louis of Battenber.g is in ours. Indeed, his passion for his pro- fession is known outside the confines of Ruesia, whi,e, in the opinion of the English colony at Petersburg, he is " the smartest man in the navy." In addition to the Grand Dukes there are a good many counts and princes holeing commissions in the Russian sea service. It is perhaps rather too fashionable, because the invariable defect of a fashionable profession enters—teat is to say, every officer does not became one for love of a sea life, and in consequence many are very anxious to snare shore-going billets. As there are many such, foreign service, especially in the Pacific, comes to he looked upon as a sort of exile to be avoided as much as possible. This feeling is not absolutely general—a crack ship like the Russia is regarded as a plum—but foreign service in Russia is looked on very differently to the way it is looked at in our Navy. A very high proportion of officers, too, are married ; and of two officers otherwise squeal the celibate ie always the most effective. That we know in our service. The theore`dcaA technical training of Russian naval officers is on a scale altogether beyond anything we have in our Navy. They study tactics and strategy regularly, not as an exotic. I came across a curious in- stance of this. Some while ago there was a good deal written abut tactics in the United Service lartitution Journal by Captain H. J. May, R N., ono of our leading authorities on the matter. But if any officer in our ser- vice is famiiitr with this Writing he is so of his own volition only. In Ressia, where they study the RUSE. Journal, the May theory of tactics is part of the recog- nised curriculum ; it is acteally better known in a foreign navy than to the navy for whom it Was origin- ally propeunded ! I could cite a dozen similar in- stances. " War game "is a recognised naval institutiou in the Russ'an Navy. All through the winter, two days a week, at the Naval Art idemy the officers as part of their reetilar training play a strategical game invented some while since, by the Grand Duke Alexander. This game covers all those minute but vital questions such as coal endurance, supplies, and so forth, and every possible contingency that the Russian Navy might be called on , to face is worked out. In the event of any meeting of hostile forces, the ensuing tactical problems are then carefully worked out by the tactical Rriegspiel associa- ted with my own name. I feel here that I am on a little awkward ground ; but the game being mare or leis officially recognised in most navies except the Britiso, it is in a way beyond my own private concern, so perhaps I may be forgiven for mentioning it. The Russians play this tactical game with full rules, a state ot things that renders the word "game "very inappro- priate. Admirals b'ay—l have never, save once, seen any admiral but a Russian doing this. For an admiral te be teaten at his own business by a junicr officer is an awkward contretemps, to say the least ; but it is bound to happen occasionally ; while with admirals new to the game, it is likely to be trequeat. There are certain erthodox formations that good and intelligent gunnery (which the Kriegspiel assumes) must I render fatal, though on paper they look unassailable. I h saw a Russian admiral so beaten, and badly baaten, by

an officer much his junior, with an inferior force better handled. Wean it was over the admiral laughed : " I should hare adopted that formation in a real battle," ho said, " alai it's better to be beaten in a shun fight than in a real one." In a real fight bad gunnery on toe enemy's par; might have made a difference—it might not ;in any case tactics built on the chances of an enemy's faults are bad. Subsequently that admiral played the same action again, alopcing other tactics and winning.

If this were all it would not necessarily amount to much. These games were some of many that we played nightly at the Zeal& Palace—from halt-past seven to one o'clock in the rn oraiug. From twelve to fifteen officers usually participated, and subsequeutly every move was discusned and argued out at the Naval Academy. It is this discussion that does the teaching, and for good or evil there it is as the characteristic of the Russian naval officers of to-day. It is not unique; the French, for in- stance, to seme extent, the Japanese to a great extent, are atte.r the same pattern, but the Russian carries it further. Of curse, there are plenty of officers in our ser ViCi who" think things out," but they have to do it more or tes individually, not with official coaching and assistance. I do not want to say more about this matter than is necessary to prove my point, but to do so fully lam rather driven to say one thing. The Rusin ad- miral to whom I have referred (he was one of man) ) is a moan of world-wide reputation, wha might very well be pardoaed if he held tnat he knew all there was to ' know. Last year I wrote to three well-known British admirals, to none of whom my name was unfamiliar, saying tnat since foreign nations were interested in it,if they would care to see the game, I would show it to them at any time they might find convenient. Two curtly said they hadn't time, the third (the Sea Loris of the Admiralty) made no reply at all beyond the offi- cial acknowledgment of receipt. The utility or otherwise of the game does not enter into this question—it is purely a question that something ta be of use was in existence, and that our people would not take the trouble to inquire into it. Altogether, I fancy these pretty little future war pictures we real abiut, where toe Russians are always beaten because our admirals are no much better at tactics, might bear a little editing. If it came to a war there are more of us, we have infinitely better opportunities tor practical training, and in the case of the sailors much longer ser- vice. In all these things we have a great pole But let us make n) mistake,there would be not merely brave men against us, but also able men who think of other things than "spit and polish."

1 ;hould make some reference to the Rus.ian Naval Intelligence Department, which is said ta be the teist in the world. From what I saw and heard there I gathered that they knew as much or more about our Navy than Mr. Gesclaen, and that they considered our Intelligence Department an " interesting institution." Tbey knew far mere about our confidential instructions thaa most of our own officers are ever allowed to know. The Russians poesess (thanks to their " N.1.D.") draw- ings of our sacredly confidential siebmerged tubes. Taey do not, however, know how to use them, but the reason why is not pretty. It is that the man who sold the information didn't know himself. It is a popular idea that tee ofice boys and porters at the Admiralty, and "mateys" in our dockyards, are Russian spies. The idea has probably little basis in fact, though no doula; some things do go to Russia ; and we do not discover times about Russia as a quid pro quo. Of course, this sort of 'dung is fess essential to the British navy than to any other, and a blessed thing for us that it is se. Our Intelligence Department is not so much to bison, because it is not allowed enough money to do anything to justify its name ; it is a well-known service yara that it an officer sends it valuable informa- tion it t.ends stamps to defray his postage, but no one as yet earned those stamps because the "N.1.D." cafi't afford it. Oa tae other hand he is pretty eertain to have been seubbed. Tue Russians work things differently, and on the whole very well. New and again their agents may romance a little in the information that they send, but this may be accidental ; no bureau can avoid occasional errors. On the whole it is an institution for the efficiency of which one can feel nothing but admira- tion, and an unpleasant amount of respect. In coeclusieu, I have in previous articles made the comparsian between the Russian and British officers as men, so there is not much snore need be added. Before all things the Russian is a saiior, in which he differs mightily from the German naval officer who is " a soldier at sea," as the Russians say. (:):herwise, be- yond the racial differences concerning whice I have a!- ready written, all naial officers are much of a pattern, the sea air produces a ceitain well-known "type." The Russian offfeer, from some strong racial similarity, pos- sibly alsa owing to thiegs inherited from those Britishers who helped to found his navy, is more like the English officer than any other. A lovable fellow he is, one can- not help liking him whether one wishes to or no. And if ever we do go to war with Russia, whatever may happen on land, at sea, if there is a battle, when it is over and the best man ha s won, there will be a good deal of friendly hand-shaking as the smoke blows away over the water. War may be very horrible and wicked, but in its modern form it has at least certain virtues, that the act of fighting (on the sea at any rate) engenders regard and ceineets it. Even the Japanese and China- men, who had an hereditary racial feud, grew fond of each other after the Homeric contests at Yalu and " Daily Chronicle."

div.p: NOTES ON dAYIE3 AND ATHLETICS.
POLICE SPORTS.

The Warrington Borough Police Athletic Club is cam- peseJ of a very energetic body of mem, and the way they go about the work for their Second Annual Sports —which are to be held in Au2ust, for the benefit of the local Infirmary and District Nursing Association— augurs well for the SUCCES3 of the undertaking. A gymnastic display was to have been given by a team from Orbrd Barracks, but owing to orders sent out by Lord Walsley they are forbidden to give a show of any kind. Nothing seems to daunt our policemen in any way, and they soon EiPt out to find substitutes to take their places. This they were successful in doing, and a team from the Warrington Gymnasium, under the direc- tion of Professor Kinsley is to give a display, and will, no dot, prove a successful venture.
A DRUNKEN ROUT AND ITS RESULT.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Thursday morning, before air. Olandley (in the chair) and Mr. John Faircleugh, Stephen Mallon, 14, King-strset, was charged with atti-mpting to commit suicide by cutting his throat on July 14%.—The Chief Constahle said de- fendant came from Ireland, and had been travelling in this country with cloth. Oa the 7ch of July he came to Warrington and went to lodge with a Mrs. K Innedy, at 14, King-street. During that week he appeared, accord- ing to hie own account and from inquiries made by the police, to have been drinking very heavily. That had undoubtedly turned h a brain. Shortly after one o'clock on Friday, the 14th, Sergeant Bell was summoned to the house by Mrs. Kennedy, who told him that she thought something was wrong with her lodger who was upstairs. The sergeant proceeded tu the bedroom and found the man lying on his face on the bed. He turned him over, and found a sever_? wound in his throat, from which blood was flowing copiously. On a chair at the bedside were a razor, and a bottle of medicine. Defendant was unconscious. The sergeant rendered first aid, and bad the man removed to the Infirmary. He had been there ever since. From what the doctor said, and from the inquiries of the police, he (the Chief Constable), felt pretty sure that the man was not responsible for his actions at the time he attemptPd to take his life, and under the circumstances he w-iu!cl offer no evidence. Defend ,ist had promised non to repeat such a foolish act, nor the conduct which led up to it.— Defendant's father said he had never known him to take drink before.—The Chief Constable said that defendant had neglected his food and been drinking spirits, with the result that he got into a very) despondent state. He thoneht that trade and everything were going against him.—Defendant's father promised to take care of him, and defendant promising not to re- peat his foolish conduct, was discharged.

div.head: FILTIIY ABODE AT FRODSEIAIL
div.p: A FILTIIY ABODE AT FRODSEIAIL
THE RESULT OF DRINK.

j At the Froisham Petty Sessions on Wednesday morn- ling, Messrs. A. Thomas (presiding), and J. Crossland Taylor, were made acquainted with the interior of a filthy abede at Prodstiana, and also with people respon- sible for the sad state ot affairs. The prosecution arose AS the result of investigations by Inspector Hackett of the N.S.P.C.C., aad again illustraees the good work that society has accomplisued for the relief of neglected children. The society was represented by Mr. A. Browne solicitor, Warrington. Alice Sangwine, 16, Booth-street, Frodsham,in answer to a charge of wilfully illtreating and neglecting her six citiliren, Thomas (13 years), William (9 years), Joseph (7 years), Lilly (4 years), Arthur (3 years), and Alice (11 months), on the 19ta July and divers other days in sues manner as to cause them unnecessary suffering mid in- jury to health, pleaded guilty. Mr. A. Bre wne, addressing the Bench, said it must not be understood by those people who were prosecutor! by the society that it was uone in antagonism to tnem it was done for their own good. In the case before them the cause could be traced atm, lutely to drink. It was a case where the husband worked hard and received good wages, averaging about 303. a week. He gave his wife 18s. a week and there were six children to ktep out of that. It was clear that the husletud was not quite blameless in the matter, and they would go so far as to say there was a waste of 7s. a week iu something or other. At present the husband was getting 253., gave his wife 183., and kept 7s. When the house, in Booth-street, was visited by Impactor Hackett and Constable Wagg, he found the woman and one child almost naked. Tue baby was nearly naked and very airty. The woman was but partially dresseo and had neither shoes nor stockings on. She was also under the influence of drink and had a pint of beer be- sides her at the time. There was no food in the house except a ham shank. The children were,however,fairly well nourished. Joseph (7 years) was filthly dreasei in pants and a wretchedly dirty old shirt ; Lilly (4) was as badly off for clothing but besides being diity was vermin bitten. Still her head was perfectly clear of vermin, and it bad been ascertaiaed that the little girl was in the habit of washing her own head although she had not the means to dry it ; Arthur, who was a very small bay for his age (3 years), was only clothed in some old rags tied together with tape ; the baby was only trussed up in an old shirt, whilst William , the elder boy, had his clothes all in rags and his body was filthy. As stated, the only food in the house was a " bone-shank," and that day the children had been obliged to go without dinner. The only money in the house, according to the woman's st itenaent, was Is 2d. The whole house was fairly furnished, but in a filthy condition. Tne interior of the back kitchen, and a back bedroom presented a sickening sight, both having been used for natural purposes by the children, with the result that it made the Inspector almost ill on beholding it. In the upstairs room the woman had made some attempt to cover the filch, but suets a state of affairs could not but be con- ducive to the distress, ill-comfort, and detriment oftthe health of herself and her children—it was cruelty to the children. There were no clothes whatever in the house, except those discovered upon the family when the visit was mad?. He hoped the bench would not take the appearance of the defend- ant that day as a criterion of her usual appearaece.—The husband called, stated defendant was "a goed wife" and " a good mother," and if they would give her another chance he was sure sho would alter—she had promised him she would never taste an- other drop while she lived.—Mr. Tayloryso the husband): What do you do with the 7s. you keep? The Husband : Ever since I have given her 18s. a week, I have found the children in shoes and other necessities out of my ' pocket money.—The Chairman (addressing defendant): It was only through drink that you neglected these children, now your husband says you will never taste it again. Is that so ?—The Husband : Oa behalf of my- self make tier sign the pledge sir.—The Chairman con- tinuing : You make up your mind not to drink again ? —Defendant : Who was crying bitterly, said" Yes."— The Chairman : Very well ; we will give you another chance, but if you come hear again you will go to prison. You must pay 203. including costs, or in de- j fault 14 days with hard labour. The money was paid.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MISS MATTHE NS, EARLESTOWN.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MISS MATTHE NS, EARLESTOWN.

St. John's Church, Earlestown, was on Saturday crowded with a very large number of people on the occa,ion of the marriage of Mies Matthews, eldest daughter of the Rev. T. R. Matthews, vicar of Earlestovvn. Miss Matthews in consequence of her long residence and connection with the town was exceedingly well-known, and much interest was accordingly evinced in the ceremony. The chancel of the church and eloir stalls were taste- fully decorated with plants and flowers, the work having been done by the church officers. Shortly before half past two the guests bege.n to assemble in the church a portion being reserved for their accommodation, and amongst those present were ' Mr and Mrs Peterson of Croaton House, cousins of 1 bridegroom,Mre Virhittenbury-Kaye(sister of bride), Mrs Holt (aunt), Mr H Peterson, Mr and Mrs Clare, Ivy Mount, Latchford, Mrs Longton, Dr Mouncey. Mr and Mrs W W Shirley, &c. The service was fully choral and during the period of waiting Mr Harrison, organist, played a voluntary. At half- past two,the bride entered the church,leaning on tbe arm of the Rev. E. Whittenbury-Kaye, her brother- in-law, and attended by her bridesmaids Miss Nelly Patterson. and Miss Winuie Blair (in the absence of Miss Mouncey who was indisposed). The bride was attired in a slate coloured silk dress, with hat to match.and the bridesmaids in white, each carry- ing floral bouquets. At the chancel steps the bride was joined by the bridegroom, Mr. John James Wil- son, of Princes Park, Liverpool, his best man being Rev. G. A. Vesey. Tbe ceremony was performed by the Rev. Dr. Royston, Suffragan Bishop of Liver- pool, assisted by the Rev. T. R. Matthews, the bride's father, the bride being given away by her brother-in-law,Rev. E. W.l'lnittenbury-Kaye, in the absence of her brother, wh) is in South Africa Prior to the ceremony the hymm, " The voice that breathed o'er Eden," was sung, and at the close "0 Christ the King of human life." A reunion was afterwards held at the Vicarage, and in the course of the afternoon the newly wedded pair left for Simmons Yacht, Herefordshire, where the honey- moon will be spent. div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

EBENEZER WHSLEYAN SIINHXY SCHOOL.—The scholars, with the teachers end friends, numbering about 208,held their annual outing on Tuesday. As in previous years, the venue chosen was Overton Hills, for which place the greater portion of the pry left the chapel at, nine a.m., in tw4 'buses, the children having been sent on pre- viously in a lurry, under the care of Mr. Spencely. An enjoyable iaurney was made in beautiful weather, Overton being reached by eleven a.m. The hills were at once climeds and no time was wasted in the pursuit of pleasure. Dinner was provided at Mersey View, after which gamea of all kinds, bowls, and the swing boats were utilized to provide amusement. The beiutiful walks on the hills were also enjoyed, the caves being visited, but wen not, however, entered. At 4 p.m, the school re-assembled at Mersey View for tea. Mesdames Moss, Ellison. and Proud, and the Misses Proud and Gc:rrarrt, presided at the tables. The arrangements for the comfort of the party, which were admirably carried out, reflected great credit on Mr. Miller (superintendent), and Mr. Brereton (secre- tary.) After a most enjoyable day spent on the heather• clad hills, the start home was made at 720 p.m., St;icktou Heath being reached about nine o'clock,

div.head: UNKNOWN SOUTH AMERICA. INTERVIEW WITH CAPTAIN DOWDING.
div.p: UNKNOWN SOUTH AMERICA. INTERVIEW WITH CAPTAIN DOWDING.

Most peopla, if they were asked to name offhand some part of to world as to whose geography we are par• ticularly ignorant, would most assuredly mention scime part of the African Continent, if they had been warned that the North an d South polar regions were barred. They might be given half a dozen opportunities of guessing, but still, unless they happened to be special- ists in geography, they would never know that the region of which least is known is a certain district in South America. It is this district which Captain Herbert C. Dowding. R.N., has been exploring, and a rapresentative of the " Morning Post " recently waited on him to interview him as to his experience. Captain Dowding started on the Eastern side at the mouta of the Orinoco, and crossed the con- tinent, and arrived at Tumaco, 'whence he took the fortnightly steamer to Panama, crossed to Colon, and thence returned to this country. Going up the Orinoco, Capt tin Dowding, who was accompanied by a botanist, Mr. Sprague, arrived at the mouth of the Meta. This is the chief tributary of the Orinoco, and the party fol- lowel its course towards the Cordilleras. Here they narrowly escaped disaster, for their boat went on the rocks and was fast filliag when she was fortunately got ashore. The cargo was removed and the boat's bottom mended. Then she proceeded to Orocue. Here a new boat was procured, and after a fortnight the ex- plorers arrived at Cabuyaro.

div.head: THU UNMEASURED LLANOS.
div.p: THU UNMEASURED LLANOS.

Around this place the Llano 3 stretch to the South. The e are huge plains civered with grass that rises to the height of the knee, and intorsected by occasional strips of dense forest. Their full extent has never been d-termined, and it was one of the objects of the expedi- tion to obtain definite knowledge as to this point. But it was absolutely necessary to have plenty of carriers if the district was to be properly explored, and the Indians at Bagoto refused to go South. Captain Dowding there- fore determined to march through the forests to S. Augustin, in the Valley of the Magdalena. The journey was exhausting in the extreme. Nothiug could lo ptocured on the way, and all the stores and instruments had to be carried. It is interesting to learn that a half-caste is capable of transporting a load of four hundredweight, while an Indian is expected to carry three. Often the undergrowth was so thick that men had to be sent on ahead to cut a way for the party, and so one is not surprised te hear that progress was exceedingly slow, thou4h there was from ten to eleven hours' marching daily. S. Augustin, when it was reach< d, proved to be exactly like some hundreis of the " towns" whose names figure in the maps of this region. It CAIII9 into being in the days when quinine WAS a cestly commodity. It has new somewhere about 20 inhabitants.
GODS AND PXOTOGRAPHY.

The forests which surround it are interesting because they contain numereus statues of forgotten gcds, who are repreßentfd as having been cannibals. Captain Dowding declares that 601119 sort of fate protects them , from the desecration of being successfully photographed- The attempt has been made more than once, and Cap- tain D leading devot, d much trouble to the task and secured several excellent negatives. What became of them will be learned later on ; suffice it for the present to say that they stand in the tangled forest and to all intents and purposes have succeeded in not being photo- graphed. Misfortune still doggeil the footstsps of the party. In the course of a fifteen days' march to Mocea, through the forests of the Cordilleras, Captain Dowdiug fell ill, and had to be carried by his Indians. Arriving at this point he parted with Mr. Sprague, who had de- cided to return by another route. He then proceeded to Paste, arriving there after tea days' travel. This is a town situated tea thousand feet above the sea in the mot beautiful part of the Cordilleras. It is two days' j urney from the Frontier of Ecuador, and eight from Quito, its capital. It is above the forests and so lies in the midst of excellent pastures, which may possibly account for the fact that it has so many as twelve thousand inhabitants. It is ninety miles as the crow flies from the coast, and this fact is mentioned because a new volcano, up to the pre- sent unnamed, has lately made its appearance at a little distance from the town in a north-easterly direction, and as Captain Dowding made his way down to the sea he found that the foliage was everywhere grey with the dust cast up and scattered by the eruption. From this point Captain Dowding made a two-days' journey to fuquerez, which lies amid scenery still magnificent at a height of 8,200 feet above the sea level. Seven days more brought the explorer to Barbacos, on the Telembi, where he got on board a steamer, and after about four hours' steaming, found himself on the waters of the Rio retie..

div.head: COMPLETE DISASTER.
div.p: COMPLETE DISASTER.

Here misfortune became disaster. Navigation was difficult, and the pilot incompetent. He ran the boat on some rocks in the middle of the river,and in ten minutes she sank. There was no one drowned, but Captain Dowding lost all his note books and all his photographs. The notes were of the utmost importance, for they in- cluded careful observations as to the latitude and longi- tude of a large number of the placbs named on the best maps of South America. These have hardly been alters.] for the last hundred years, and in almost all casn the towns are wrongly located. Often by the bye, they are hardly to be called towns, being simply places utterly uninhabited, which happen to possess names, whiih they got from to earliest Jesuit missionaries There were valuable barometric records as to the alti- tudes of various places, and data which would have en- abled the makers of maps to correct hereafter their re- pre6eatations of the course of certain rivers. But they all lie at the bottom of the Rio Patia. After this crown- ing misfortune Captain Dowding took a canoe from Sala Hunda—whieh lay just beyond the scene of the accident and proceeded through the mangrove swamps to th,, sea, and so, as has been said above, to Tumace. His account of the region traversed is exceedingly fascinat- ing. The man who would fain add to the stock of human knowledge has only to ad venture thither with a small stock of instruments in order to obtain facts for which geographers will be devoutly grateful.
A PRIMITIVE COUNTRY.

Travel through the forests is immensely difficult; but it is full of interest. Tne flowers are marvellous ; the birds are like the most gorgeous of flowers. The coun- try is famous for its snakes ; and if the naturalist is in want of specimens he has only to give his orders to an Indian boy,and they are to hand ahnost immediately. Yet the ordinary traveller has no need to fear them. It only he is careful to walk noisily whenever he finds himself in doubtful places he will be as safe as if he were wandering in English meadows. For the most venomous snake does not use its weapons except in self-defence ; and it is significant that Captain Dowd- ing saw no snakes beyond a few which had been killed by the people who went ahead of the party. Again, it is frequently alleged that the black tiger is an aggressive b^ast, which will on occasion attack men. Captain Dowding has twice crossed the South American Con- tinent, and his path has frequently been cut through virgin forests, where the animal presumably abounded. He has never come across it, and those who desire to do so must obtain the services of a skilled huntsman, and exercise a deal of patience. As to the people, they are primitive in the extreme. Everybody is very poor, as is only natural in a country where you get twenty paper dollars for an English sovereign.

div.head: FRUGAL FARE.
div.p: FRUGAL FARE.

Even the people who are comparatively well-to-do never allow themselves the luxury of what we should recognize as beef. They get nothing better than the flesh of an old cow which has been killed because she has ceased to give milk. This is boiled for a little while,and the liquid is called soup. The stringy half-cooked flesh is eaten with relish, but anyone accustomed to English food will find it utterly impossible to swallow it, mile people are extremely lazy, and are quite content to live, two hundred years 13.3 hind the times, in the places where they were born. If any man among them is extraordinarily enterprising he journeys South to the had waters of the Caqueta Biver and traffics in caoutchouc. This he conveys to the West Coast over the Cordilleras, because there is a thirty per cent duty on indla rubber at the mouth of the Amazon. M-rchandise is universally carried by pack horses, whicn do as much as 16 miles a day "if the road are not unusually bad." During the whole of his j?urney across the continent Captain Dowding saw only one rudimentary cart. It consisted of a plank on the roughest of wheels, and would probably have collapsed under half the load which a half-brei d is expected to carry. It was nevertheless lecally regar- ded as an amazing novelty, and wherever it went tho people turned out to inspect it, precisely as English ruitics used to do a year or two ago if a motor car passed through the village they inhabited. It may be added, in conclusion, that the country is the last refuge of ultramontanism. The priests are almost ;omnipotent among those whose spiritual welfare is in their charge. Tney are devoted ministers, and Captain Dowding has to remember unnumbered kindnesses received at their hands.

BIG FIRE IN MANCHESTER. A TRAMP WARD GU TTED. TERRIBLE LEA_YS OF INMATES.

A fire brose out 5 esterday morning at the tramp wani of the Man,hester and Cnorlton Union. The building was found to be alight on toe third and fourth storeys. Seven or eight tramps were in the upper rooms, and were cut off from the main staircases and unable to use the iron staircase outside the building. There was no- thing for it but to jump. Life sheets were held by the firemen, and an excited crowd looked on. Seven men leaped trona the fifth storey, an enorm ms height, and another was able to use a life-line. All wore more or less injured, and were at once conveyed to Anc )ats Hospital. The efforts of the firemen to quench tne flames were usekss. Tne building W 43 entirely gutted, and at noon only the four walls were standing. CHILDREN BITTEN 131 I MAD DOG. A mad dog rushed through Pontardulais,a village near Llanelly, on Wednesday evening.and attacked a number of email children, inflicting terrible injuries about the face. Seven children were badly bitten, tb• eye of an orphan boy being torn out, and it is feared that his re- covery is hopeless. The villagers followed the infuriated animal to a butcher's yard, wnere, alter further attack- ing a labourer, it was chained and snot by the police. THE LYNCHING OF ITALIANS. INDEMNITY TO BE PAID. NEW YORK, TRIIRMAX.

The " Herald's" Wasnington correspondent telegraphs that Italy will be paid an indemnity f,)r tbree of the five victims of the Tallulah lynching affair. The State Department lays down the principle that an alien does not become a citizen of the United B:ates until naturali- sation papers have been formally issued.

A ST. ANNES MYSTERY. laformation was given to the police at St. Annes on Wednesday night, that a man's body was lying on the saw:Mills near the Ormerod Convalescent Home. Ser- geant Blackburn went, and with constables, removed tne body, to wait an inquest. N Clue to the deceased's identification has been found. His age is about thirty. He is well dressed, of medium height, has dark brown hair and moustache, sallow complexion, grey ay( s, wore a black cJat and vest, anti grey striped trousers. A blue macintosh was lying near him. Tne collar bore the name "Cox, Alexandra Road,Manchester." DISASTROUS CHESHIRE FARM FIRE. GREAr DESTRUCIION OF STACKS. At eight o'clock yesterday morning one of the most disastrous stack fires which have ever taken place in Cheshire occurred on the largest farm on Lady- Tabley'S estate, that of Mr. Isaac Farish, Mirston Hall, tear Northwich. Threshing operations were in progress ig the yard, which contained seven stacks of hay, corn, and straw, when a boy noticed some catch fire.probably with a spark from the engine. In a moment the flamee enveloped the whole of the stack had spread with great rapidity to other stacks, which contained about 20i tons of hay and 100 tons of unthreshed and threshed straw. There was only time to save the engine and presser. The Northwich fire brigade arrived about a quarter to nine,but the stacks were beyond redemption, and they confined their efforts to playing on the ad- j Aning building. Furtner inquiries elicit 'that the outbreak has proved more extensive than was at first thought. The darn- , age which is covered by insurance is roughly estimated at £2,000. Altogether eight stacks have been totally destroyed as well as valuable implements including a I large chopping machine which cost about £l2O. The scene of tie conflagation which can be seen for many miles round has been visited lisy hundreds of people. YESTERDAY'S CRICKET. CLOSE OF PLAY SCORES. I LANCASHIRE v. THE STANLEY BENEFACTION. Canon WILLIS announced that the Rectors of Bury, Winwick, and Warrington had given the Stanley bene- faction to the Rev. J: 0. Coleman, of Bolton. Canon PENRHYN moved a vote of thanks to the Chair- man which was cordially passed and the meeting closed. SERVICE AT THE PARISH CHURCH. Divine service was afterwards held in the Parish Church. when the preacher was the Rev Canon Willink, vicar of St. Helens. THE LUNCHEON AND TOASTS. Later, luncheon was provided in the Clergy Daughters' School, the arrangements for which were very satisfactory. The CHAIRMAN (the Dean of Manchester) said he must express their deep regret at the absence of Sir Francis Powell who had!been detained by his duties in the House of Commons He(the speaker) proposed tFae toast of '‘The Church and Queen." Speaking of the Queen,he said he regarded her in the light of the greatest personality of not merely this country but of the world. (Hear, hear.) Captain WITHINGTON proposed the toast of the" The Bishops, Clergy, and the three Dioceses." He was sorry to see there was not one of the three bishops present to respond. • Archdeacon GORE, in responding, after alluding to the toast, said tbe headmistress who presided over the school had that morning been pre ented with a beautiful bouquet (exhibiting it) by the pupils of the school. No better testimany to their effection for her could be shown, and no bette: evidence of the work done by Miss liennedyiwas needed. The CHAIRMAN prop ,sed the toast of the" Warring- ton Institution," and referred to the religious instruction at the School. Under the direction of the Rev. Morley Stevenson the religious knowledge was imparted and there was no better man in the whole of England, and he was there to say on behalf of H.M.'s Inspectors there was no better ciPege in England, nor one that was de- lug better work than the one in Warrington. Canon BLACKBURN respended. He was quite certain if some wealthy man would listen to the circumstances of their case he would feel for them. It was a great com- fort to see on even' side the great work being done. Mr. FULLAGAR proposed the toast of "Their preacher, Canon Wiilink." Capon %%MUNK expressed the pleasure it gave him to come to such an excellent church as the Parish Church they had at Warrington. Canon BLACKBURN proposed the concluding toast, "The town and trade of Warrington," which was cordi- ally received. DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES. A concert was given by the pupils later in the after- neon. An excellent programme was gone through for which they w.are deserving of great praise. At the con- clusion Canon Gore presented the prizes to the success- ful pupils.

PROSECUTIONS • FOR BREACHES OF THE FACTORY ACTS. TWO WARRINGTON FIRMS SUMMONED. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, last Friday, before the Mayor and other magistrates, two local firms were summoned at the instance of Mr. .1. H. Rogers, one of Her Majeety's Inspectors of Factories, for breaches of the Factory Acts. The first ease heard was that in which Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., Limited, of Atherten's Quay, were sum- moned for eaving on the 26th May, employed two young persons named William Webb and James Hands later than six o'clock in the evening. Mr. Rogers said he appeared for the Home Office to prosecute two firms for offences against the Factory Acts. Messrs. Monks Hall and Company were charged with employing two young persons after legal hours at their tube works. Au inspector visited the place on the 28th of May just before eight o'clock and found the boys at work. They had frequently worked over- time,and on this occasion one was instructed to work ' until nine. The Act stipulated twelve hours and the hours of work at this place were from six o'clock to six. It was very important that these boys should not work overtime. They penalty was £3 in each case. Mr. Smith, a factory inspector, gave evidence as to his visit to the works and finding the boys working at sixteen minutes to eight. He spoke to the watchman but he could not see the foreman.—By Alderman Roberts : Did von speak to any official ?—I told the watchman to inform the menager.—Ele would not be the person in charge would he P—The foreman was away at the time. Councillor Burton, manager of the firm, who now ap- peared on behalf of the company, having been delayed by the 'bus, said that with respect to Hands, the magis- trates would Pe by the declaration book he now pro- duced, that he was 18 years and one month old. The form was signed by Dr. White. With regard to Webb he had no instructions from the foreman to work over- time. He had not the slightest id;a there was any lad working. Mr. Rogers, after examining the entry in the book, said he would like an anjournment in order that the birth certificate might be produced. Alderman Roberts; Is not the declaration sufficient to extlude tee firm from all liability in the matter. It is signed by the Medical Officer ? Mr. Roger.: It is not properly fined up. James Elands was then called and said he had"turned eighteen years of age. He could not say when he was' born. He admitted that he told the inspector he was 17 years of age. Councillor Burton said he bad the birth certificate with him. Mr. Rogers said this dccument showed that Hands was born on the 25th April, 1382, BO that he must be more than 1 years of age. He would withdraw the ease against the firm respecting Hands and pay the costs. On the charge of employing Webb, the firm was fined 5s and costa, 193 6el in all. Alb4rt Payne, builder, Liverpool-road, was then ebareed with employing a boy after legal hours. on May 26h, named Harry Waywell.—Mr. Parkinson said Mr. Payne was unable to appear in person. Mr. Recers stated that this was a similar offence to she previous case. Ihe boy was found working at 7.20 p.m. He had signed a declaration that he was six- teen years of age ; that he commenced work at six o'clock in the morning and that he had been working on sash and door frames since six o'clock in the evening. He had worked overtime each night during the week until 7.30. Mr Smith said he saw the boy working at the time stated. He was sand-panering, sash frames. Harry Ws vwell, 16 years of age, also gave evidence. The magistrates said they considered this a worse case than tes last and fined the defendant 10a and costs, £1 43 61 in all.
